It said Islanders were victims of an invasion in 1982 that left many traumatised, making the banner particularly insensitive, and stated that its policy is not to see politics brought into sport, nor the Islands used as a “political football” in every conversation between England and Argentina. It expressed hope that FIFA would sanction such behaviour in line with its own rules.

Argentina maintains a sovereignty claim over the Islands, administered by the United Kingdom since 1833. In the 2013 referendum, residents voted overwhelmingly to retain their status as a British overseas territory.

Fernández, 25, remains the subject of speculation about a departure from Chelsea. The club set an asking price of around 120 million pounds and received no bids before Friday's deadline.

World.title: The Washington-Tehran memorandum expires without talks ever having opened
World.content:
The Washington-Tehran memorandum expires without talks ever having opened

17th Monday, August 2026 - 23:07 UTC Full article

US President Donald Trump ruled out renewing it and described the deadline's expiry as irrelevant, saying there is no set timetable

The memorandum of understanding signed on June 17 by the United States and Iran expired on Monday at the end of its sixty-day term, without the peace talks it envisaged ever taking place and without either side announcing an extension.

US President Donald Trump ruled out renewing it and described the deadline's expiry as irrelevant, saying there is no set timetable. “They want to make a deal, but they are not going to make the kind of deal I consider necessary,” he told reporters in the Oval Office. On his social network he wrote that the primary goal is and always will be to prevent Iran from having a nuclear weapon.

Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei gave a different account of the failure. He said the deadline had become obsolete because of violations Tehran says Washington committed weeks after signing. “We have not entered into any negotiations,” he said.

The text required Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and to reaffirm that it will not acquire or develop nuclear weapons, while the United States undertook to lift its naval blockade and sanctions. Around 20% of the world's oil passes through the strait.

The waterway remains the main sticking point. Trump on Monday threatened to bomb Oman, a US ally, if it obstructs any eventual agreement. “If Oman gets in our way,” he told Fox News reporter Trey Yingst, the country would face strikes. Asked about it later in the Oval Office, he did not soften his position: “They are not behaving very well.”

Muscat and Tehran have been negotiating for weeks, without US participation, a mechanism to manage shipping traffic through the strait. Baghaei said there is an understanding on the transit route map and that both sides are finalising a joint declaration. The agreement would not, however, mean reopening: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said early this month that reopening depends on additional conditions, and deputy minister Kazem Gharibabadi said the strait “will only be closed and opened under Iran's command” and that the blockade will continue until Washington accepts what he described as its defeat.

On the ground, the cycle of attacks and reprisals continues. Last week US forces disabled the Panama-flagged container ship Vela Nova in the Gulf of Oman for attempting to head to an Iranian port. US Central Command has redirected 55 commercial vessels, disabled three and boarded two since reimposing the blockade on July 14.

A Reuters poll released on Monday puts Trump's approval at 33%, the lowest of his second term. The conflict began on February 28.

World.title: Colima’s Pouleth Carbajal swims the English Channel
World.content:
Pouleth Carbajal swam from England to France in a little more than 14 hours over the weekend, becoming the first person from the Mexican state of Colima to complete a solo English Channel crossing.

The 24-year-old native of Manzanillo, Colima, left Shakespeare Beach, near Dover, at 2:12 a.m. Sunday and that afternoon reached the dunes at Wissant, France, according to the Channel Swimming & Piloting Federation (CS&PF).

The federation listed her unofficial time at 14 hours, 7 minutes. Mexican reports said she covered 65.3 kilometers, or about 40.6 miles, as currents extended her route beyond the channel’s narrowest straight-line distance of about 21 miles.

Carbajal was coached by Sandra Venegas Ortiz, and her support team included Gabriela Cuero, her mother. Listed as an observer was Karina Almanza, a swimmer from Mexico City who herself completed the English Channel in 2018.

Carbajal’s swim remains subject to official ratification, but the federation called it an “unofficial success” and congratulated her “on a great swim.”

In a Facebook post, the Manzanillo municipal government called her accomplishment “a source of pride for Manzanillo,” adding that Carbajal showed that “with discipline, preparation and determination, it is possible to achieve great challenges.”

The English Channel is among open-water swimming’s best-known endurance tests, requiring swimmers to contend with cold water, tides, currents and some of the world’s busiest shipping lanes. In Spanish, the waterway is called the Canal de la Mancha, derived from its name in French, La Manche, “the sleeve.”

The CS&PF database lists 3,384 solo channel swims by 2,728 swimmers, and historical data cited by Britannica put the average successful crossing time at roughly 13 hours, 34 minutes.

The one-way record is 6 hours, 45 minutes and 25 seconds, set by Germany’s Andreas Waschburger in 2023. The women’s record is 7:25:15, set by Czech swimmer Yvetta Hlaváčová in 2006.

According to the English Channel Swimming database, Carbajal’s swim, once ratified, will become the 88th Mexican solo crossing of the channel.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Jorge Padilla Castillo (@jorgepadillacst)

That list includes a pair of two-way, over-and-back crossings — Nora Toledano Cadena in 1994 and Carlos Alfonso Acosta Aldrete in 2023; both are from Mexico City.

Another prominent Mexican open-water swimmer is David Olvera, a San Luis Potosí native who swam nonstop from Cozumel to Cancún earlier this year, and last year set a Guinness World Record for the fastest circumnavigation swim around Manhattan Island (5:34.58).

Patricia Guerra from Mexico City completed the same course around Manhattan (7:53.12) in August 2023, a month after swimming the Strait of Gibraltar between Spain and Morocco.

With reports from El Heraldo de México and Milenio

World.title: Deadly Sonora heat wave expected to intensify over next 3 days
World.content:
Temperatures are expected to exceed 40 degrees Celsius (104 degrees Fahrenheit) for the next three days in the northwestern border state of Sonora, with highs reaching 47 C in municipalities in the northwest and central region, according to Mexico’s National Meteorological Service (SMN).

The dangerous heat wave, which has lasted more than six weeks, has already caused 22 deaths and sickened 350 as of Tuesday morning, reports the Sonora state Health Ministry.

Temperaturas máximas registradas la tarde de ayer en estaciones de #Sonora

El valor mas alto que se presentó fue de 46.9°C en El Pinacate.

Fuentes: @ConaguaOCSonora, @CESAVE_Sonora. pic.twitter.com/XPq10IkZJH — Gilberto Lagarda Vas (@gilbertolagarda) August 18, 2026

The cities of San Luis Río Colorado, Caborca and Hermosillo could experience highs of between 43 C and 47 C. In the state capital of Hermosillo, the relative humidity is around 45%, while the ultraviolet radiation index is in the “extreme” category, ranging from 8 to 11.

The SMN is also monitoring summer monsoon conditions, with isolated storms reported in the mountainous regions of central and southern Sonora.

The State Civil Protection Coordination announced that monsoons will continue to bring rainfall across much of Sonora on Tuesday but will not cause temperatures to drop. Residents can expect moderate to heavy rain, lightning and gusty winds.

Construction and agricultural workers have been warned to take precautions, and employers are urged to schedule breaks during the workday to allow workers to hydrate and reduce their exposure during peak sun hours.

Health authorities are encouraging the public to stay hydrated, wear light-colored, lightweight clothing with long sleeves and use a hat or umbrella to protect themselves from the sun. People should avoid being outdoors during the hottest hours of the day, with older adults and children at greatest risk.

The main signs associated with heatstroke (golpe de calor) include severe headache, dizziness, confusion, nausea, very hot skin and loss of consciousness. Health authorities have advised the public to seek immediate medical attention by calling 911 if these severe symptoms occur.

With reports from La Jornada and El Sol de México

World.title: Navy seizes over 300 IEDs and 300 kg of explosives in Sinaloa
World.content:
The Mexican Navy on Tuesday said that its personnel had seized more than 300 improvised explosive devices (IEDs) and around 300 kilograms of explosives in a southern municipality of Sinaloa, a state where IEDs have been used in the long-running battle between rival factions of the Sinaloa Cartel.

The Ministry of the Navy (SEMAR) said in a statement that navy personnel found the IEDs and explosive material near Agua Verde, a small town in Rosario, a municipality that borders both Nayarit and Durango.

Como parte de las acciones para fortalecer la seguridad en Sinaloa, en El Rosario, elementos de @SEMAR_mx localizaron más de 300 artefactos explosivos improvisados y cerca de 300 kg de explosivos. Personal naval especializado aseguró la zona y deshabilitó los artefactos en el… pic.twitter.com/QfhWrg0wJ5 — Gabinete de Seguridad de México (@GabSeguridadMX) August 18, 2026

The discovery was made at a rural property during an operation led by the navy in conjunction with the federal Security Ministry and the Federal Attorney General’s Office.

SEMAR said that the area where the IEDs and explosives were found was cordoned off and that specialized personnel from the Navy’s Explosive Devices Search, Location and Neutralization team defused the devices “on site.”

“Through these actions, the Ministry of the Navy, via the Mexican Navy and in coordination with agencies of the [federal] Security Cabinet, helps to improve security conditions,” SEMAR said.

The ministry reaffirmed its “commitment to continue carrying out operations to uphold the rule of law and ensure the safety of Mexican families.”

SEMAR didn’t report any arrests in connection with the discovery of the IEDs and explosives.

This week’s bust came just over two months after state and federal security authorities located more than 550 IEDs at another property in Rosario. Significant numbers of IEDs have also been seized in other parts of the state, including in the municipalities of San Ignacio, Culiacán and Badiraguato, where convicted drug trafficker and former Sinaloa Cartel leader Joaquín “El Chapo” Guzmán was born.

The artisanal explosive devices have been used by the Los Chapitos and Los Mayos factions of the Sinaloa Cartel during their bloody conflict, which intensified in 2024 after Ismael “El Mayo” Zambada was kidnapped by one of El Chapo’s sons, Joaquín Guzmán López, and forced onto a plane that flew him and Guzmán López to New Mexico, where both men were arrested by U.S. authorities. IEDs have also been used in Sinaloa to attack homes, businesses and police.

According to the newspaper Milenio, authorities seized 5,298 IEDs in Sinaloa last year, the highest number of any state in Mexico. Citing information it obtained via a freedom of information request, Milenio reported in February that the Mexican military and National Guard seized more IEDs across Mexico last year than ever before. The total number of IEDs seized by the military and the National Guard last year — 9,802 — represented an increase of 272% compared to 2024.

The increase in the use of IEDs — and authorities’ seizure of the devices — has been linked, in part, to the conflict between Los Chapos and Los Mayos. Other Mexican criminal groups, including the powerful Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG), also use IEDs against rival organizations and authorities. After Sinaloa, the state where authorities seized the highest number of IEDs last year was Michoacán, where various crime groups, including the CJNG, operate.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: How Guanajuato became the setting for a modern ‘Don Quixote’
World.content:
Producing a modern-day film adaptation of the novel “Don Quixote” in Guanajuato is something only an idealist would undertake, especially a newcomer to Mexico with limited Spanish. But that’s exactly what Paul Smart, a filmmaker, writer and radio producer from New York’s Hudson Valley, chose to do when he moved to Guanajuato in 2021 with his wife, Fawn Potash — a photographer and encaustic artist — and their son.

The “Cervantes Capital of the Americas,” Guanajuato has long been considered Don Quixote’s home outside Spain. Its annual international performing arts festival, Cervantino, is the biggest in Latin America, and the city’s Museo Iconográfico del Quijote houses the world’s largest collection of art inspired by the novel.

As Smart got to know Guanajuato, strolling its labyrinthine alleys, he fell in love with the city’s “grand vistas and the layered mixture of old and new, European and Indigenous, beautiful and utilitarian,” he said.

He started reading up on local and national history, becoming so enthralled by the city’s connection to Don Quixote that he produced a 175-episode radio reading series of the novel, punctuated with pieces of music and personal reflections. It aired on listener-supported radio stations in the U.S.

“I failed Don Quixote in college,” he says in the first episode. “I was an English major, and it was in Spanish. I made fun of it.”

Today, Smart sees many parallels between Don Quixote’s quest to reinvent himself and his own midlife musings.

How the film ‘Don Barry: A Quixotic Exploration’ was conceived

After the radio series, Smart was ready for another project — but still haunted by Don Quixote — and began imagining a contemporary version of Cervantes’ classic.

“I felt nicely challenged by the fact that ‘Don Quixote’ is known for killing the ambitions of many a great director,” he said.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Indiecinema | Independent Films (@indiecinema.co)

As he played around with a script, the image of an old friend came to mind. Barry Gerson was an 80-year-old experimental filmmaker and, like Quixote, a quirky and impractical idealist. Smart created a composite character, “Don Barry,” by mashing together the two men, one real and one fictional.

He used Cervantes’ own words from the novel’s second book, which deals with mortality and creativity.

In ironic timing, while Smart was noodling ideas, he got a call from Gerson. His friend had been experimenting with color LED therapy lights to cure himself of “the maladies of aging” — diabetes, prostate cancer and the onset of dementia. Gerson had 20 pages of detailed handwritten notes that he thought might be publishable.

Would Smart help him?

Smart suddenly realized that Gerson’s anti-aging experiments were the exact material for “Don Barry,” and the film began to take shape. Ultimately, Gerson flew to Guanajuato, and Smart shot the film in real crowds, using local dancers and musicians, during the 2023 Cervantino Festival and Day of the Dead. A young Mexican animator and physicist, Genda Monter, played a modern-day Sanchia (based on Sancho Panza), Don Barry’s assistant.

How to produce a film in Mexico without much Spanish

“I speak minimal Spanish. ‘Como un bebé,’” Smart said he tells people. But he knows how to make himself understood.

“The trick is to read a person’s eyes, smile a lot, move your hands and bring in a translator when possible.”

He also avoids places where English is spoken, “to try to activate the language center I still think exists somewhere within me.” He worked on “Don Barry,” for example, in cafés in the working-class city of Irapuato, where his son went to school for two years. You don’t hear much English in Irapuato.

Collaborating with a local producer and local camera people also helped. “We had paperwork explaining what we were doing, including various agreements for people to sign.” People understood. “I paid out a lot of 200- and 500-peso notes for release signatures, which made everyone happy,” he added.

Challenges beyond language

Gerson was not an easy person to work with.

“He didn’t tell me he could barely walk,” Smart said, “and he couldn’t remember lines. And first he had me build him an LED-light rehab studio in his Airbnb.”

A tight budget was another issue, since Smart was largely self-funding the project. Festival fees ran more than US $100. But after he began exhibiting in small cultural centers, “Don Barry” started winning accolades.

The film has been shown in Guanajuato, Mexico City, Austin, Portland, the Hudson Valley and Italy, and is available on Prime Video.

What’s next for Smart

Now, Smart is writing a script for a new film called “Six-Seven: Playing with Magic,” about two girls from the U.S. and two boys from Mexico, ages 5 to 7, who play together over a summer, a period that they remember a few years later in the film.

“Like ‘Don Barry,’ the film is about aging, but seen from childhood instead of old age,” Smart said. His goal is to show the film this winter at festival premieres that have already honored him.

Smart is not only a filmmaker and radio producer, but also the author of the memoir “With Different Eyes: A Covid Waltz in Words and Images.” He has also written a novel: “Overlook: A Rock and Roll Fable.”

He believes that nurturing creativity is much easier in a country like Mexico, where capitalism is less “predatory” than in the U.S., and where not all values are economic.

“One of the first things I saw and appreciated here was the way all elements of life are allowed to coexist … the ugly and beautiful, life and death, rich and poor, dirty and clean. Some call it surrealism, others a wider appreciation of life,” he wrote in an email.

Whichever it is, the rich, heady atmosphere in Mexico provides the oxygen that enables Smart to keep creating.

Louisa Rogers and her husband Barry Evans divide their lives between Guanajuato and Eureka, on California’s North Coast. Louisa writes articles and essays about expat life, Mexico, travel, physical and psychological health, retirement and spirituality. Her recent articles are available on her website, authory.com/LouisaRogers.

World.title: Spanish police confiscate dozens of critically endangered Mexican axolotls
World.content:
Spain’s National Police have recovered 29 axolotls, a critically endangered amphibian endemic to Mexico that survives in the wild only in the canal system of Xochimilco in Mexico City.

Spanish authorities confiscated the specimens in the city of Granada and are investigating a Mexican national for his alleged participation in illegally trading the axolotls.

Although the International Union for Conservation of Nature classifies the axolotl as a critically endangered species — the category immediately preceding extinction in the wild — its international trade is legal, though strictly regulated.

The species is included in Appendix II of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora. As such, international trade must be controlled and supported by the necessary documentation to prove the legal origin and traceability of the specimens.

Spanish authorities say the suspect did not have the proper documentation. Therefore, they seized the axolotls and are pursuing charges of unauthorized possession and sale of specimens of a protected species.

Meanwhile, the axolotls are under the supervision of specialized veterinary personnel at the Zoobotanical Biodiversity Conservation Center of Jerez de la Frontera, in Cadiz.

The natural population of axolotls in Mexico has suffered a marked decline as a result of habitat destruction and degradation, water pollution, urban sprawl and the introduction of invasive species into the Xochimilco canal system.

This precarious situation contrasts sharply with their growing popularity as pets, making it especially important to control the origin of these carnivorous amphibians and prevent demand from fueling their illegal trade.

Even so, Mexican media have reported that axolotls are illegally sold (for around 500 pesos, or US $30) at the Mixhuca Market in the Venustiano Carranza borough of Mexico City.

In addition to Europe, the illegal trade reaches as far as South America, where Chilean officials confiscated 65 axolotls in April. Chilean officials have estimated that nine in 10 axolotls die of asphyxiation, dehydration or exposure to extreme temperatures during the transition.

Although appreciated as exotic pets, a lack of adequate information and unsuitable captive conditions endanger the lives of these amphibians. Placing an axolotl in a fish tank with clean water overlooks the reality that they are an extremely delicate species with very specific needs.

With reports from LopezDoriga.com, El Heraldo de México and N+

World.title: Cox to build US $310M desalination plant in Baja California
World.content:
Spanish company Grupo Cox will build a long-awaited desalination plant in Rosarito, a coastal city in the drought-prone state of Baja California.

The National Water Commission (Conagua) last week awarded a 5.29 billion-peso (about US $310 million) contract to Cox to build both a desalination plant and its pumping station in Rosarito, a town located south of Tijuana on the Pacific coast. The company submitted a bid for the project as the leader of a consortium that includes Mexican company Gami Ingenieria e Instalaciones.

Cox, which has a Mexican subsidiary called Cox de México, acknowledged Conagua’s decision in a statement released on Monday.

“Cox, an international group specializing in critical water and energy infrastructure, has been awarded, through a public tender process, the construction of the Rosarito desalination plant in Baja California, Mexico,” the company said.

“The project, promoted by the National Water Commission (Conagua), represents an investment of US $304 million and will help strengthen water security in the region, benefiting one million people during its first phase,” said Cox, which evidently calculated the cost in dollars using an outdated USD:MXN exchange rate.

The company said that the plant — which has been in the works for years — is “one of the priority initiatives under Mexico’s National Water Plan and will address the water supply needs of Playas de Rosarito and the south-western area of Tijuana.”

Enrique Riquelme, Cox’s executive chairman, said that the desalination plant project “reaffirms our commitment to Mexico following the acquisition of Iberdrola Mexico.”

“Through this award, we are bringing our expertise in the water sector to a country where we continue to support the development of infrastructure that contributes to people’s well-being and to the country’s sustainable growth,” he said.

“We are proud to collaborate with federal and state authorities on an initiative aligned with the objectives of the National Water Plan and one that will help strengthen the region’s resilience to the challenges associated with climate change,” Riquelme said.

Cox: Desal plant will produce 190 million liters of drinking water per day in first phase

Cox said that the first phase of the project includes the construction of a desalination plant with the capacity to treat 2,200 liters of seawater per second, “enabling the incorporation of approximately 190 million liters of drinking water per day into the regional water supply system.”

The company said that construction of the plant is expected to be completed in three years.

“Cox will be responsible for the engineering, procurement of specialized equipment and construction of the infrastructure, which will provide a complementary and independent water source from the Colorado River, strengthening water resource availability in Baja California,” Cox said.

“The desalination plant will have a final production capacity of 4,400 liters per second, equivalent to more than 380,000 m³ [380 million liters] of drinking water per day, making it the largest facility of its kind in Latin America,” the company said.

Cox said that the plant will use “reverse osmosis technology, an advanced treatment system that employs semi-permeable membranes to remove salts, minerals and impurities from seawater and convert it into drinking water.”

This technology is recognized for its high operational efficiency, the quality of the water produced and its lower energy intensity compared with other desalination solutions,” the company said.

Cox noted that it operates desalination plants across 16 countries with a combined desalinated water production capacity exceeding 4.4 billion liters per day.

The public tender process

Cox’s 5.29-billion-peso bid for the desalination plant project was the lowest among three participants in Conagua’s public tender process.

The score for its proposal — 94 out of 100 — was higher than those given to one consortium led by Acciona Agua México and another led by Tecno Arrendamientos y Construcciones.

The federal and Baja California governments will jointly fund the desalination plant.

Two previous tender processes for the desalination plant failed to find a company that was able to meet the technical and economic requirements of the project. Consolidated Water was previously contracted to build the plant, but the Baja California government canceled the company’s contract in 2019 and a lengthy legal dispute ensued.

With reports from Expansión, El Sol de México, EFE and BNamericas

World.title: Bilateral security cooperation nets more fugitives, including several priority US targets
World.content:
U.S.-Mexico cooperation on security matters has netted another criminal destined for extradition, sending a clear message: “Whatever the crime, criminals have nowhere to hide.”

Jalisco police officers captured a man identified as Antoni Covarrubias in Puerto Vallarta who was considered a priority target by U.S. authorities. Covarrubias, 41, is wanted on charges of second-degree murder in California.

U.S.-Mexico security coordination continues to deliver results. Through close cooperation between 🇺🇸 & 🇲🇽 authorities, Jalisco Police arrested a fugitive wanted in the United States for murder and other serious crimes. The cooperation advanced by @POTUS @realDonaldTrump and… pic.twitter.com/xVoKAlvceP — Embajador Ronald Johnson (@USAmbMex) August 17, 2026

In a social media post, U.S. Ambassador to Mexico Ronald Johnson praised the cooperative effort of Mexican authorities, highlighting the positive results derived from bilateral security coordination.

Illustrating these recent successes, Johnson announced a few hours later that U.S. authorities had “turned over six more fugitives wanted in Mexico for serious crimes, including murder and firearms offenses, with one linked to a narco-terrorist organization.”

The operation in Puerto Vallarta was carried out in coordination with the U.S. Marshals Service after Jalisco authorities received information about the fugitive’s whereabouts in the heart of the popular tourist resort.

With the help of drones and the C2 Mobile Cybertruck, state police and a tactical unit were deployed to the area. According to police reports, Covarrubias was apprehended after a brief chase without incident.

A search of the suspect turned up quantities of marijuana and crystal meth, but charges of drug possession were set aside once it was confirmed that the man was the target sought by U.S. authorities.

State officials contacted the U.S. Marshals Service to begin procedures to hand Covarrubias over for extradition.

On Monday, Ambassador Johnson posted a photograph of the detainee, handcuffed and guarded by four Jalisco police officers, and declared “criminals have nowhere to hide.” The apprehension of Covarrubias is reportedly the ninth arrest of a high-profile U.S. target in the state of Jalisco in recent weeks.

In recent days, U.S. authorities turned over six more fugitives wanted in Mexico for serious crimes, including murder and firearms offenses, with one linked to a narco-terrorist organization. As the cooperation advanced by @POTUS @realDonaldTrump and President @ClaudiaShein… pic.twitter.com/SDhwqeAtIv — Embajador Ronald Johnson (@USAmbMex) August 17, 2026

This spate of captures and extraditions includes the return of three fugitives to Mexico over the weekend. The three suspects — including one who is allegedly a member of the notorious Jalisco New Generation Cartel — were wanted by Mexican authorities on a variety of criminal charges, including murder.

On Sunday, Johnson said the success demonstrates that effective security collaboration sends a clear message to criminals: “You will be caught and you will be held accountable.”

Also last week, the U.S. Marshals Service announced that Mexican authorities had deported one of Texas’ 10 Most Wanted fugitives who was wanted on multiple state and federal charges.

At the same time, Mexican and U.S. authorities conducted a rapid-response binational security exercise along a highly visible stretch of El Paso-Cd. Juárez border area.

With reports from La Jornada, LatinUS, Noticias Puerto Vallarta and Debate

World.title: Sheinbaum says fuel smuggling is ‘over’ in Mexico: Tuesday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Listen to this article

Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

🇺🇸 Sheinbaum sticks to her “political” reading of AMLO’s son’s visa revocation: Asked whether Andrés Manuel López Beltrán had ever been on authorities’ radar over huachicol fiscal , the president said flatly, “he was not,” and repeated that the cancelation of his U.S. visa is a political matter and a case of “interference in the decisions of Mexico.”

Asked whether Andrés Manuel López Beltrán had ever been on authorities’ radar over , the president said flatly, “he was not,” and repeated that the cancelation of his U.S. visa is a political matter and a case of “interference in the decisions of Mexico.” 🎯 Opposition is using the case to “attack” the government, president says: Because the opposition “has no plan for the country,” Sheinbaum argued, it has seized on the revocation to attack “the project that we represent,” with a barrage of criticism from the right, pundits and media outlets after López Beltrán made the cancelation of his visa public in a letter to U.S. President Donald Trump.

Because the opposition “has no plan for the country,” Sheinbaum argued, it has seized on the revocation to attack “the project that we represent,” with a barrage of criticism from the right, pundits and media outlets after López Beltrán made the cancelation of his visa public in a letter to U.S. President Donald Trump. ⛽ Fuel smuggling “practically over,” according to the president: Sheinbaum said her administration has all but ended huachicol fiscal thanks to interventions in customs and a series of arrests. She complained that government critics ignore that progress in favor of using visa revocations of Morena officials as a political weapon.

Sheinbaum said her administration has all but ended thanks to interventions in customs and a series of arrests. She complained that government critics ignore that progress in favor of using visa revocations of Morena officials as a political weapon. 🚫 “There was no list”: Defending legal adviser Luisa María Alcalde, Sheinbaum denied that a “blacklist” of journalists was presented at last Wednesday’s “right of reply” press conference. She said that Alcalde simply showed how stories from reporters such as Ciro Gómez Leyva, Joaquín López Dóriga, Ana Paula Ordorica, Azucena Uresti and Carlos Loret de Mola are amplified on social media to “create an opinion trend.”

Why today’s mañanera matters

The revocation of the U.S. visa of Andrés Manuel López Beltrán, a son of ex-president Andrés Manuel López Obrador and the former secretary of organization for the ruling Morena party, continues to be a major topic in the national conversation. The revocation came after dozens of other Morena officials, including Baja California Governor Marina del Pilar Ávila, were also stripped of their U.S. visas.

At her Tuesday morning press conference, President Claudia Sheinbaum once again offered her opinion on the situation amid calls from the opposition National Action Party (PAN) for López Beltrán to be investigated for alleged involvement in a tax evasion/fuel smuggling scheme known in Mexico as huachicol fiscal.

Today’s mañanera was also significant as Sheinbaum weighed in on another issue that has received significant attention in recent days. That issue is the presentation by presidential legal adviser Luisa María Alcalde of a list of high-profile journalists and media outlets whose critical coverage of the government is said to be amplified online in order to attack the federal government and the “fourth transformation” political movement that Sheinbaum leads.

Sheinbaum reiterates view that revocation of López Beltrán’s US visa was politically motivated

A reporter noted that the Federal Attorney General’s Office said on Monday that it has no proof that would warrant the commencement of an investigation into allegations that López Beltrán is involved in fuel-related crimes. He asked the president whether López Beltrán was ever on authorities’ “radar” for alleged involvement in huachicol fiscal.

“He was not,” Sheinbaum responded.

“And as I mentioned on Friday, from our point of view this is a political issue,” she said, referring to the revocation of López Beltrán’s U.S. visa.

“It’s not related to other issues,” Sheinbaum said.

Rather, she said, it’s a matter of “interference in the decisions of Mexico.”

“… There are other criminals, or alleged criminals, let’s put it that way, where there is no problem [with their U.S. visas],” Sheinbaum said.

“Or there are other politically exposed persons, as they call them, where it’s the other way around — they open the doors to them,” she said.

“I’m not going to name names because I don’t want to get into a controversy,” Sheinbaum said.

Sheinbaum: Opposition is using revocation of López Beltrán’s visa to ‘attack’ the government

Sheinbaum asserted that “as the opposition has no plan for the country,” it uses the revocation of López Beltrán’s visa to “attack the project that we represent.”

“They take away his visa, he decided to make it public with a letter [addressed to U.S. President Donald Trump] and then the barrage of criticism came from the conservative side of politics, from the right, from the pundits, from the media outlets,” she said.

Sheinbaum: Government has ‘practically’ put an end to huachicol fiscal

Sheinbaum asserted that her administration has “practically” put an end to “huachicol fiscal, or the smuggling of fuel.”

“It’s practically over thanks to the interventions that we’ve been carrying out in customs and the arrests that have been made,” she said.

Sheinbaum said that government critics don’t talk about the progress the government has made in combating huachicol fiscal.

Instead, they use revocations of Morena officials’ U.S. visas to attack the government, she reiterated.

“They have the right to do that. Nobody is going to censor them as they claim we will, but it is necessary to point out the work that has been done [to combat huachicol fiscal],” Sheinbaum said.

Sheinbaum defends her top legal adviser amid claims she disseminated a ‘blacklist’ of journalists

A reporter raised remarks made by Luisa María Alcalde at the “right of reply” press conference she held last Wednesday.

🔴La presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum repitió que “no hubo ninguna lista” de periodistas. Explicó que los nombres de periodistas mencionados por Luisa María Alcalde buscaban mostrar cómo las redes sociales y plataformas digitales pueden amplificar información y generar tendencias de… — Azucena Uresti (@azucenau) August 18, 2026

She asked Sheinbaum whether Alcalde, a former interior minister and national president of Morena, had not “directly blamed” certain journalists for initiating an “offensive” against the government because she said that those journalists are the source of anti-government messages that are subsequently amplified on social media, including by bots.

Alcalde faced significant criticism for presenting a so-called “blacklist” of journalists who are said to be opposed to the federal government. In addition, video footage of Sheinbaum saying in 2021 that the drawing up of lists of political adversaries is a practice of McCarthyism and Nazism was widely shared on social media.

On Tuesday morning, Sheinbaum asserted that Alcalde did not in fact present a list at her “right of reply” press conference, a relatively new initiative of the federal government.

“First, there was no list,” she said.

“Names were presented — what Luisa presented … what she showed is the use of digital platforms, of social media, to amplify a piece of news and even create fake news,” Sheinbaum said.

“That’s what she presented,” she said.

Sheinbaum said that Alcalde showed how “a piece of news from these journalists” — among whom were Ciro Gómez Leyva, Joaquín López Dóriga, Ana Paula Ordorica, Azucena Uresti and Carlos Loret de Mola —can be amplified on social media to “create an opinion trend.”

“There are multiple cases of this that we can talk about, many cases,” she said. Narco-government, narco-candidate, narco-president, all that,” Sheinbaum said.

The president went on to say that her government defends the right to free speech.

“Who here has been censored? Give me the name of a journalist we’ve censored,” Sheinbaum said.

“There isn’t one. Tell me the name of a media outlet we’ve censored. There isn’t one,” she said.

World.title: El Niño Deepens Costa Rica’s Divide Between Drought and Heavy Rain
World.content:
Costa Rica is experiencing two sharply different rainy seasons at once, with a growing drought across the Pacific side and Central Valley while unusually heavy rainfall affects the Caribbean. The National Meteorological Institute (IMN) has confirmed that meteorological drought now covers the entire Pacific slope, the Central Valley and the western Northern Zone, including areas around Upala, Los Chiles and Guatuso.

The latest climate outlook, which runs through February 2027, offers little sign of a substantial recovery in the driest regions. El Niño is expected to remain strong through August and could reach “very strong” intensity between September and November. “This El Niño will remain strong through August, but from September through November, it is expected to intensify into a ‘very strong’ El Niño,” said Karina Hernández, a specialist with the IMN’s Climatology Unit.

That classification describes the warming of the equatorial Pacific Ocean, not necessarily how severe the effects will be in Costa Rica. A strong El Niño involves ocean temperatures more than 1.5 degrees Celsius above average, while the threshold for a very strong event exceeds 2 degrees Celsius.

Hernández said current measurements are already above those recorded during the 2015 El Niño event, although the warming trend has remained relatively stable during the past two months. If the event intensifies further, the final quarter of 2026 is the most likely period because El Niño typically reaches its peak toward the end of the year.

The effects are already visible in Costa Rica’s rainfall totals. The Pacific North could finish August with up to 80% less rain than normal. Deficits of roughly 60% are projected for the Central Pacific, South Pacific and Central Valley, while the western Northern Zone could receive about 40% less rain.

The shortfall has expanded considerably since July, when drought had been confirmed in the Central Valley, the western Northern Zone and much of the North Pacific. At that time, the IMN was still monitoring the Nicoya Peninsula, Osa Peninsula and parts of the Central Pacific. Those areas have since fallen within the broader drought zone.

Meteorological drought does not mean that rain has stopped completely. Some communities may still experience downpours and thunderstorms, but isolated heavy rainfall may not be enough to compensate for months of accumulated shortages.

The IMN also does not declare drought after only a few dry weeks. Its assessment requires sustained rainfall deficits across several weather stations using complete 30-year records. The conditions must persist through three consecutive moving three-month periods, representing roughly five months of deficient rainfall.

As of now, the designation refers specifically to meteorological drought. If the dry pattern continues, it could eventually develop into agricultural drought, affecting soil moisture and crops. A longer and more severe shortage could later affect rivers, reservoirs, drinking-water supplies and hydroelectric generation.

On the other hand, the Caribbean is facing the opposite problem. For August, rainfall is forecast to reach approximately 60% above normal in the Northern Caribbean and 40% above normal in the Southern Caribbean. The eastern Northern Zone could receive around 30% more rain than usual. From September through November, the Caribbean is expected to record about 15% more rainfall than normal. Totals in the eastern Northern Zone should remain closer to their usual range.

This difference is characteristic of El Niño’s effects in Costa Rica. The phenomenon generally reduces rainfall and raises temperatures along the Pacific and in the Central Valley while directing more moisture toward the Caribbean. Temperatures are also expected to remain well above normal. The IMN projects increases of between 1.5°C and 2°C (2.7°F and 3.6°F) across the Pacific, Central Valley and western Northern Zone. The Caribbean and eastern Northern Zone could run between 0.5°C and 1°C (0.9°F and 1.8°F) above average.

Costa Rica has already registered a series of heat records. Thirteen weather stations recorded historic maximum temperatures during July, followed by 14 records on August 11. Temperatures reached 37.5°C (99.5°F) in Santa Cruz and 37.2°C (99°F) at Finca La Ceiba in Nicoya. The contrasting outlook means Costa Rica must prepare for both sides of the same climate pattern: prolonged water shortages and pressure on agriculture in the Pacific, alongside a heightened risk of flooding, saturated soil and landslides in the Caribbean.

World.title: Guanacaste Airport Outpaces Costa Rica’s Main Airport
World.content:
Costa Rica welcomed more than 2 million international tourists during the first seven months of 2026, but the clearest sign of change was not simply how many people arrived. It was where they chose to land. Guanacaste Airport in Liberia recorded the strongest airport growth, reinforcing its role as the main gateway to Costa Rica’s northern Pacific beaches.

For those heading to Tamarindo, Playas del Coco, the Papagayo Peninsula or other parts of the Nicoya Peninsula, flying into Liberia can eliminate the need to cross the Central Valley and then make the long drive west. The airport’s expanding network of direct flights is making that option available to more visitors.

A total of 698,079 international tourists entered Costa Rica through the Guanacaste airport between January and July, an increase of 13.3% from the same period in 2025. In July alone, the airport received 89,947 visitors, up 12.6%. Juan Santamaría International Airport remained Costa Rica’s busiest entry point, welcoming 1,154,732 international tourists during the seven-month period. Arrivals at the Alajuela airport grew by 3.6%, including 158,076 visitors in July.

Together, the two airports accounted for most of the 2,001,660 international tourists who visited Costa Rica from January through July. The overall number was 6.4% higher than during the same period last year. Air travel continued to power the tourism industry, accounting for 1,853,430 arrivals and growing by 7%. Another 142,780 visitors entered by land or water, although arrivals through those routes declined by 1.7%.

The figures also reveal a gradual shift in where Costa Rica’s visitors are coming from. The United States remained the largest tourism market by a wide margin, sending 1,142,234 visitors during the first seven months of the year. Americans accounted for 57% of all international arrivals, but growth from the United States was almost flat at 0.4%.

That makes the performance of other international markets increasingly important. Canada recorded one of the strongest increases, with 220,691 Canadian tourists arriving between January and July, up 24.4%. Costa Rica also received 315,340 visitors from Europe, an increase of 8.4%.

Arrivals grew from North America, South America, Europe, the Asia-Pacific region, the Caribbean and the Middle East. Visitor numbers from Central America and Africa declined. The July results also brought some relief after tourism arrivals slipped in June. For hotels, vacation rentals, restaurants, transportation providers and tour companies, continued growth heading into the year-end high season would be welcome.

Still, the gains are not evenly distributed. Costa Rica’s tourism growth is increasingly being driven by Guanacaste Airport and markets such as Canada and Europe, while the much larger U.S. market remains largely unchanged. More than the two-million-visitor milestone, that changing pattern may be the most important tourism story of 2026.

World.title: What happened to Galeria Namu?
World.content:
Founded in 1998, Galeria Namu had become a must-visit attraction for tourists visiting San Jose, as well as for many nationals, interested in seeing the gallery’s curated collection of authentic ethnographic and cultural arts of Costa Rica and then, on the 30th of December, 2024, Namu was suddenly forced to shutter the gallery indefinitely.

This article is for folks who, since December 2024 – right at the beginning of Costa Rica’s annual high tourist season – would have walked up, expectingly, to Galeria Namu’s entrance on the edge of Barrio Amon, right across from the Alianza Francesa (the French Alliance) on Avenida 7, just to be met with the sad sight of the permanently shuttered locale. The large billboard still up on the wall, with its distinctive Pre-Columbian-inspired logo, would have given pedestrians the sense that the gallery was still open for business.

With the change of the building’s ownership in 2024, the gallery, that September of the same year, was given notice that the new owners were not going to renew the lease in the new year as they had “other ideas” for the space (read: we want to increase rent for another business!).

With this unexpected closure of the gallery, so ended nearly three decades of a cultural “institution” that strove, under a fair-trade business practice, to offer to a discerning public, a marvelous catalogue of Costa Rica’s national cultural arts and authentic ethnographic material culture (a subject matter, that frankly, for a highly visited Central American nation, is somewhat undocumented even today).

The good news is that Galeria Namu still exists, albeit, for now, in a digital format, with the official website having been launched in March of this present year. Namu is still receiving new pieces all the time in the three arts categories that the gallery collection has always showcased:

1. Ethnographic material culture and artistic expression created by artisans from among the 8 indigenous groups of Costa Rica

2. Faithfully rendered, museum-quality reproductions of Pre-Columbian era objects, such as those seen in the exhibition halls of the national museums, featuring goldwork, authentic jade pieces, pottery and carved stone sculpture

3. Selected Costa Rican folk arts and artes populares created by artists from different milieu, such as Afro-Caribbean traditions, artisans from campesina communties, women’s art collectives, Criollo traditions, etc. – plus other individual folk artists that “fit the bill” who wonderfully depict, through their compositions, la tiquicia and the peculiarities of Costa Rican lifeways and ambience.

Aside from the primary focus on the cultures and lifeways of Costa Rica, Galeria Namu has always given a space for some examples of indigenous cultural expression from our neighbouring naciones hermanas of Panama (ie. the Wounaan tribe), Nicaragua (ie. the Miskitu people) and Honduras (ie. the indigenous Lenca).

Just as Galeria Namu has always done over the last three decades, purchased artwork can be securely packaged for international shipping and for clients who either reside in Costa Rica, or for visitors at their accommodations, the gallery is happy to get one’s purchases to one’s residence, or hotel, free of charge – or even rendez-vous in person to hand deliver purchased artwork to clients within the GAM.

https://www.galerianamu.com/

World.title: 19-year-old pleads guilty to unlicensed Glock so sister can go free; third sibling remains at large
World.content:
19-year-old pleads guilty to unlicensed Glock so sister can go free; third sibling remains at large

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 19-year-old Belize City man has been remanded to the Belize Central Prison after pleading guilty to keeping a firearm without a gun licence, while the charge against his older sister was withdrawn.

Aaron Ayren Pitter, 19, and his sister, 20-year-old Gregoria Veronica Pitter, were escorted to the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Tuesday, where they were jointly charged in connection with a Glock 17 Gen 4 9mm pistol found during a police search of a Pitter Street residence.

Aaron initially pleaded guilty while Gregoria pleaded not guilty. The Magistrate, however, declined to immediately accept Aaron’s plea and encouraged him to seek legal advice before making the decision.

The siblings were initially remanded, but minutes later Aaron requested to be brought back before the court and again indicated that he wanted to plead guilty and accept responsibility for the firearm.

His guilty plea was accepted, and he was remanded to the Belize Central Prison until September 30, 2026, when he is expected to be sentenced following mitigation.

Following Aaron’s guilty plea, the prosecution withdrew the firearm charge against Gregoria and she was released.

Police say a third sibling, Roy Pitter Jr., remains at large.

According to police, officers from the Violence Protection and Enforcement Team executed a search warrant at a residence on Pitter Street on Monday, August 17.

During a search of the bathroom, police allegedly found a pair of blue short pants stuffed inside a hole beside the bathtub. Wrapped inside the clothing was a Glock 17 Gen 4 pistol with a magazine attached.

Police say Aaron arrived at the residence while the search was underway and, after being shown the firearm, allegedly told officers that it belonged to him and that he knew it was there.

The firearm and magazine were examined and found to contain no ammunition.

Aaron and Gregoria were subsequently detained and charged with keeping a firearm without a gun license.

World.title: Belize City fisherman remanded after allegedly sneaking into ex’s house through bedroom window and slapping her after breakup
World.content:
Belize City fisherman remanded after allegedly sneaking into ex’s house through bedroom window and slapping her after breakup

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 32-year-old Belize City fisherman has been remanded to the Belize Central Prison after being charged in connection with an alleged domestic dispute involving the mother of his children.

Ramzee Roman Palma, also known as “Terral Palma,” appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court, where he was charged with burglary with intent to cause bodily harm and harm upon a 30-year-old woman.

The harm charge stems from an alleged incident on Friday, August 14, while the burglary charge relates to an incident the following day.

Palma pleaded not guilty and maintained in court that he had not entered the woman’s home. The Magistrate cautioned him against saying more about the allegations while unrepresented, explaining that he could potentially incriminate himself.

The prosecution objected to bail, citing the serious nature of the burglary allegation and concerns surrounding domestic violence cases.

Palma pleaded with the court for bail, telling the Magistrate that he has three children at home and that his imprisonment would negatively affect his family. The Magistrate, however, upheld the prosecution’s objection and remanded him to prison until October 13, 2026. He was informed of his right to apply to the High Court for bail.

According to police, the Gender Violence Response and Investigation Unit responded to a report on New Road early on August 14 and spoke with the woman, who reported that she and Palma had recently separated after being in a relationship for approximately eight years.

The woman alleged that at about 3:00 a.m. she was awakened by the sound of her bedroom window being opened and saw Palma entering the room without her permission.

She told police that an argument subsequently developed and Palma allegedly slapped her to the right side of her face, causing pain and swelling.

Police say officers observed swelling to the woman’s face and issued her medico-legal forms. A statement was recorded, and Palma was subsequently detained and charged with burglary and harm.

World.title: Former Treasury cashier fined $1,500 for stealing $5,000 from Government; Says she did it for ‘medical reasons’
World.content:
Former Treasury cashier fined $1,500 for stealing $5,000 from Government; Says she did it for ‘medical reasons’

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A former Government of Belize Treasury Department cashier has been fined after changing her plea to guilty in connection with the theft of $5,000 in government funds in 2024.

Shamira Hope, 35, of South Street, Belize City, appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Tuesday, where she pleaded guilty to theft.

Hope had initially pleaded not guilty after being charged in 2024 but changed her plea when the matter returned to court.

As a first-time offender for theft, Hope was spared a custodial sentence. The Magistrate fined her $1,500, along with $5 in court costs. She has until November 27, 2026, to pay the $1,505 total or, in default, serve three months in prison.

The case dates back to October 2024, when officials at the Treasury Department discovered that $5,000 was missing from Hope’s cash pan.

According to the case facts, a finance officer conducted a cash check on October 2, 2024, and discovered that 100 fifty-dollar notes, totaling $5,000, were missing.

The officer reportedly confronted Hope about the missing money, and Hope allegedly admitted that she had taken the funds for medical reasons.

An assistant accountant general subsequently reported the matter to police.

Hope was later detained and taken to the Raccoon Street Police Station. Police say she declined to participate in an interview and was subsequently charged with theft.

World.title: Baghdad Street farmer gets 3 months in jail for crack pipe and unpaid fines; Tells court he does drugs because he is in consistent pain but agrees to rehab
World.content:
Baghdad Street farmer gets 3 months in jail for crack pipe and unpaid fines; Tells court he does drugs because he is in consistent pain but agrees to rehab

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 59-year-old Belize City farmer has been sentenced to prison after pleading guilty to possession of a crack pipe and admitting in court that he has a drug addiction.

Norman Anthony Bernard, a resident of Baghdad Street, appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court, where he pleaded guilty to possession of utensils used for smoking a controlled drug after police reportedly found him with a metal crack pipe on Friday, August 14.

During mitigation, the Magistrate questioned Bernard about his history of drug-related convictions and asked whether he needed help with a drug problem.

Bernard admitted that he struggles with drug addiction, telling the court that he uses drugs because he suffers from persistent pain.

“I sick, so when I smoke drugs, it ease the pain. I smoke because I have pain all deh time,” Bernard told the court.

The Magistrate sentenced him to two months’ imprisonment and asked whether he was willing to participate in a drug rehabilitation program while incarcerated. Bernard agreed to enter the program.

The court also noted that Bernard had an outstanding $305 fine from a previous conviction, toward which he had made no payments. A warrant was sent to the Belize Central Prison requiring him to serve three months in default of that unpaid fine.

That three-month term will run concurrently with the new two-month sentence, meaning Bernard is expected to serve a total of three months in prison.

World.title: “Markhelm Lizarraga must go”: UDP doubles down after union support
World.content:
“Markhelm Lizarraga must go”: UDP doubles down after union support

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The United Democratic Party says it welcomes Belize’s trade unions joining its call for the immediate removal of Markhelm Lizarraga as Chairman of Belize Telemedia Limited.

In a statement released today, the party said it was the first to demand Lizarraga’s removal after the BTL Board approved the proposed $80 million SMART/SpeedNet acquisition.

“Our position remains clear: public assets require public accountability,” the release states.

The UDP argues that Cabinet’s later rejection of the deal does not settle the matter. According to the party, the rejection “does not erase the Board’s decision or absolve its Chairman or the appointing Government of responsibility.”

The party is again calling for Lizarraga’s immediate removal, framing the issue as one of governance rather than politics.

“This is a matter of governance. Markhelm Lizarraga must go,” the statement concludes.

The proposed acquisition drew sustained public criticism before Cabinet turned it down. BTL is majority owned by the Government of Belize, and the party maintains that decisions taken at the board level on that scale demand a public accounting.

The UDP has not indicated what further steps it will take if the call is not met.

World.title: Cayo CET opens registration for Advanced Bartending Level 3
World.content:
Cayo CET opens registration for Advanced Bartending Level 3

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The Cayo Centre for Employment Training is now accepting registrations for its Advanced Bartending Level 3 course, starting September 28, 2026.

The course runs Monday to Friday at the Cayo CET campus in two shifts, 8am to 12pm or 4pm to 8pm. It covers 100 contact hours over four weeks and is delivered by qualified and experienced instructors.



Applicants need at least two years of bartending experience, or a Tourism Hospitality Management Level 2 certificate.

The full course costs $800 and includes theory and practical sessions, educational trips, a bartending competition, and all materials. Participants who complete the programme receive a Cayo CET Level 3 certificate.

Bartending professionals will taste, evaluate, and grade the cocktails and beverages prepared by participants during the course.

Registration is open now. Interested persons can call 611-2944 or 824-2944, or email [email protected].

World.title: Police stopped him for riding upstop then found 0.2 grams of crack on him; $200 fine
World.content:
Police stopped him for riding upstop then found 0.2 grams of crack on him; $200 fine

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 51-year-old Belize City man has been fined $205 after pleading guilty to possession of 0.2 grams of crack cocaine.

Elroy Mark Bonnell, a labourer of Castle Street, appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court, where he was charged with possession of a controlled drug.

Bonnell pleaded guilty and told the court in mitigation that he did not intend to waste the court’s time.

“I got caught with the drugs. I plea guilty. Am asking for a fine,” he told the court.

The Magistrate fined Bonnell $200, along with $5 in court costs. He was given until September 30, 2026, to pay, or in default, serve one month in prison.

The charge stems from an incident on Sunday, August 16, 2026.

Police say officers were conducting motorcycle patrol on Cleghorn Street when they noticed Bonnell riding contrary to traffic with a grey shirt wrapped around his head.

Officers stopped him and informed him that a search would be conducted. Police allege that when an officer removed the shirt from Bonnell’s head, a small cream-colored substance suspected to be crack cocaine fell from the shirt to the ground near his feet.

The substance was later weighed at 0.2 grams.

World.title: ‘Ah get bust’: ‘Dads’ fined $805 for 1 gram of crack but says he can afford it
World.content:
‘Ah get bust’: ‘Dads’ fined $805 for 1 gram of crack but says he can afford it

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 61-year-old Belize City man has been fined $805 after pleading guilty to possession of one gram of crack cocaine.

Louis Alfonso Romero, a labourer of Plues Street, appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court, where he was charged with possession of a controlled drug.

Police say Romero was found in possession of one gram of crack cocaine on Sunday, August 16, 2026.

Romero wasted no time in pleading guilty to the charge.

In mitigation, he told the court that he was working and could pay a fine, adding, “Ah get bust, ah get bust.”

Romero, who is not a first-time offender, was handed a non-custodial sentence and fined $800, along with $5 in court costs.

He has until December 30, 2026, to pay the total $805. In default of payment, he faces three months’ imprisonment.

World.title: Jamaica edge Aruba 1-0 in CFU U14 competition
World.content:
KINGSTON, Jamaica — Jamaica made it two wins in a row at the Caribbean Football Union (CFU) Under 14 Boys Tier 1 Challenge Series in Punta Cana, Dominican Republic on Tuesday, edging 10-man Aruba 1-0 to maintain their lead in Group C.

After failing to score in the first half, the first time they were held scoreless in any half over the past two tournaments, Christian Foster came off the bench to score the game’s only goal.

Jamaica are on six points, three more than St Kitts/Nevis who rebounded from their loss to Jamaica to beat Curacao 4-2 in the other Group C game.

It was a physical encounter with the referee issuing at least five yellow cards and a red to Aruba’s Sebastian Wever, a second half substitute, late in the game.

Foster scored the winner after he was left unguarded in the middle of the goal and finished off a good team movement, firing a cheeky back heel pass from Tai-Sean Headley past goalkeeper Deymar Mercado Carrillo six minutes into the second half.

Jamaica will complete their first round schedule on Wednesday when they play Curacao, starting at 12:30pm, Jamaica time.

— Paul A Reid

World.title: Hospital death probe
World.content:
An undated photo of Kenise Dunn, who died at the St Ann’s Bay Regional Hospital five days after giving birth.

ADMINISTRATORS at St Ann’s Bay Regional Hospital say they have launched a probe into the death of Kenise Dunn, who died at the facility five days after giving birth.

With family demanding answers into the circumstances surrounding Dunn’s death, the hospital’s Chief Executive Officer Dennis Morgan told the Jamaica Observer on Monday that with internal investigations ongoing the hospital is not able to provide a statement on the matter.

According to Morgan, the investigation is integral in allowing all the facts to be found and confirmed, and for the family to be given factual answers.

Morgan added that the hospital could not legally disclose information about any patient to anyone who is not listed as their next of kin, and the administrators are already in contact with the relevant family member who has been cooperative with staff as the investigation continues.

Acknowledging the concerns held by the wider family, Morgan advised other relatives of Dunn to reach out with their questions either by calling or visiting the hospital, where they will be welcomed and briefed as best as possible.

But for Kirk Hall, uncle of the deceased, information surrounding the death of Dunn is long overdue.

Hall charged that since Dunn, who he affectionately called Punky, was admitted to hospital on July 29 up until her death on Friday, August 14, the medical staff interacting with her have not been willing to provide any information.

Tearfully recounting his niece’s last days, Hall on Monday told the Observer that Dunn, who was eight months’ pregnant, complained to him on July 27 about intense stomach pains and not being able to pass her stool for at least three days.

When told of her complications, Hall referred her to the hospital for checks to rule out anything beyond simple constipation and to ensure she received the necessary treatment.

He said when checking on his niece during her stay at the hospital he was still unable to get any information from the medical personnel as to what was causing her pain.

“When she went down there she called me and said, ‘Uncle Kirk, they might have to admit me.’ Days gone by and I asked what was going on, and she said, ‘The doctors, they keep just coming and pulling blood.’ Every day they just kept pulling blood from her while her belly continued to hurt,” said Hall.

“I said, ‘Punky I know how you feel, but it soon over.’ She called me last week, Friday [August 7] morning. So all this time, from the 29th, she has been there up ‘til when she called me…nothing had been done to her,” claimed Hall.

According to Hall, the numerous blood tests she had informed him of never provided any results, and his only update was that Dunn needed to do an ultrasound at a nearby medical facility, but no ambulance was available and the hospital was short-staffed.

“She said to me, ‘Uncle Kirk, they are supposed to carry me to go do an ultrasound. I hear the nurse just come and tell me they’re short of staff so they are not going to carry me, and the ambulance is not going to work.’ So I said, ‘Punky, what do you mean by they are short of staff and don’t have an ambulance?’ I said, ‘I’m coming to you either tomorrow or Sunday,’ ” Hall added.

He told the Observer that his Sunday visit was only more worrisome as Dunn, 33, could not tell him what was wrong with her and doctors refused to speak with him.

“When I saw her, she was on the stretcher and everything, but I can tell you, she was in pain. I said, ‘Punky, what happened?’ She said, ‘Uncle Kirk, I feel pain, man. Pain, pain, pain.’ So I said, ‘What did the doctor say?’ She said, ‘I can’t talk to them no more. You go ask them, ask them what happened to me.’

“So I went to the nurse and I asked her, ‘What’s going on with her? Can I speak to the doctor behind you?’ The nurse told me to have a seat, and about 10, 15 minutes later she came back and said the doctor says my niece can talk [for herself] and I’m not the next of kin, so she can’t talk to me,’ ” relayed Hall.

Following his visit he received a call from Dunn the next day that she was being taken to have the ultrasound done. By Tuesday it was revealed to him, by a relative who he says works at the hospital, that she had given birth.

Shortly after, he said he was told by that relative that a doctor advised him that she needed emergency surgery.

According to Hall, on that day, August 9, Dunn was placed on life support.

He said doctors briefed the family that she was gravely ill, after surgery revealed a tumour believed to be cancerous that was found in her colon. Hall charged that compounding her afflictions, the doctors said they removed the colon, and two litres of stool from her body after a bowel rupture.

Dunn never recovered, passing away five days later.

Now, the family is overcome by grief and riddled with questions. Why was the family not told about the results from the blood tests or the ultrasound? Why was she allowed to give birth naturally after being admitted for constipation? Was it ever confirmed that the tumour was malignant; was there a biopsy done? Was there even, ever a tumour?

Hall’s frustration was palpable, his voice breaking as he became overcome by emotion.

“We have requested all of that. We were told on Saturday that an investigation is going to be launched. This morning [Monday], persons from the Ministry of Health reportedly went in and seized all form of records when it come to her and the doctors, whatever they said and did to her and all of that. She didn’t deserve to die like that, man. Had there been proper care and compassion she wouldn’t die, man,” charged Hall

“We are waiting with bated breath to see what the findings are, what the results are,” Hall added.

World.title: Robinson sounds alarm on Jamaica’s economy
World.content:
ROBINSON... we will continue to agitate, we will continue to recommend and we will continue to hold the Government accountable so that Jamaica can have a better economy.

Opposition spokesman on Finance Julian Robinson says Jamaicans are facing a worsening cost-of-living crisis while the economy struggles to grow, blaming the Andrew Holness-led Administration for failing to take decisive action to ease the pressure on households.

Robinson, who was speaking at the annual constituency conference of fellow People’s National Party (PNP) parliamentarian Phillip Paulwell, at Vauxhall High School in Kingston Eastern and Port Royal on Sunday, said the economic challenges facing Jamaicans are being compounded by rising energy costs and the slow pace of recovery following Hurricane Melissa.

Robinson acknowledged that Hurricane Melissa, which struck Jamaica on October 28, 2025, would inevitably have affected economic activity, but argued that the Government’s response to the disaster had worsened the economic fallout.

“We have had two consecutive quarters of negative growth which means we are in a recession. We are likely to have a third quarter of negative growth and the main reason why the economy continues to flounder, we knew we had Hurricane Melissa which would have triggered at least one quarter, but the very slow pace of recovery by the Government is what is contributing to the negative growth. It is taking too long, particularly for those who are in the affected parishes in the west, to get the assistance so that they can get back on their feet,” argued Robinson.

He pointed to the latest Ministry of Finance report, which he said showed a $28.6-billion shortfall in tax revenues, and charged that the gap would place additional pressure on Government finances and force it to either reduce expenditure or dip into the capital budget. He also blamed the shortfall partly on the slow pace of assistance to hurricane-affected businesses.

But Robinson’s criticism extended beyond the impact of Melissa.

He linked the country’s economic difficulties to the cost of energy and the vulnerability of consumers to movements in global oil prices.

According to Robinson, Jamaica could do more to cushion households and businesses against higher oil prices by expanding its use of renewable energy.

“They have not added one megawatt of renewable energy to the grid. What has been done in the last 10 years is what we started when we were last in office. So while you can’t control the price of oil, you can control how much renewable energy is added to the grid and they have failed miserably at adding whether it is solar, whether it is wind,” he pointed out.

Robinson also criticised the Government’s decision to abolish the oil-price hedge, arguing that consumers have not been given another mechanism to shield them from sharp increases in fuel prices.

Beyond the immediate pressure on household budgets, Robinson said the economy was also struggling with a mismatch between the skills employers require and the workers available to fill those positions.

“We have not heard any policy or programme to deal strategically with what employers are bawling about when they say they can’t find people to work, even though every one of us as representatives can point to hundreds, maybe thousands of people who are looking for work. So there’s a clear mismatch between what employers want and what is in the market,” he said.

Robinson proposed that the Government provide financial grants to employers to train and up-skill their workers, arguing that businesses themselves are best positioned to identify the specific skills and training needed to address the gap between the skills employers require and those available in the labour market.

He ended his remarks by insisting that the Opposition would continue to press the Government on its economic policies while offering alternatives that, “could improve growth and living conditions”.

“We will continue to agitate, we will continue to recommend and we will continue to hold the Government accountable so that Jamaica can have a better economy that will suit not just a few people but all of Jamaica,” declared Robinson.

World.title: Triple L, Rytikal encourage with Keep On Fighting
World.content:
Rytikal.

For producer Triple L, music has always been about more than creating infectious rhythms. With his latest production, Keep On Fighting, featuring dancehall artiste Rytikal, he is using sound to speak directly to people navigating the pressures of everyday life.

The track, set for release on August 21 via Triple L Records, is rooted in the realities Triple L says he sees around him, from financial pressures, other stresses, and disappointment.

“[It was inspired by] real life. I see too many people around me getting knocked down but still getting back up. Dealing with bills, stress, and doors closing in their faces. I wasn’t trying to complain about it. I wanted to create something that tells people that the pressure isn’t here to break you; it’s here to build you. Keep on fighting,” he said.

For Triple L, Rytikal was an obvious choice to deliver the message because of his ability to connect with songs rooted in struggle.

“Because he has lived it. He doesn’t just sing about struggle; he feels it. When he gets on a track like this, you believe him. He has the pain and the fire. He is one of the voices for people who are tired but still standing,” he said.

The collaboration came together organically.

“I built the track specifically for him [Rytikal] and reached out to my cousin, who has a better connection with him than I do. Once that connection was made, it was a wrap,” said Triple L, adding, “I built the rhythm from a real place. He heard it, he felt it, and the energy just matched. When two people are fighting for the same purpose, things can come together quickly.”

The resulting production is deliberately raw and forceful, combining the weight of the drums with a more hopeful melodic element.

“This isn’t soft music; this is warrior music,” he said. “You can hear the streets in it, but you can also hear the future. It was made to move speakers and move minds, bodies, and souls.”

At the heart of Keep On Fighting is a message of personal responsibility, resilience, and self-worth, particularly for young people.

“Stop making excuses. Man up. Do what needs to be done. Life is going to knock you down, but you don’t have to stay there,” he said. “To the youth, know your worth. You are not what the streets say you are. Keep on fighting. Diamonds are made under pressure.”

The producer said the decision to release the project independently reflects his wider vision of building from the ground up while maintaining ownership of his work.

“We’re not waiting for anybody to believe in us. We’re putting our own work out there and owning our masters. From the bottom to the top,” he said.

Distributed by VPAL, Triple L also sees Keep On Fighting as a progression in his development as a producer. While his earlier work focused heavily on rhythms and beats, he believes the new production represents a deeper understanding of how instrumentation can carry a message.

He believes the song’s universal theme will allow it to resonate well beyond Jamaica, pointing to the fact that struggle is something shared by people regardless of their background.

“Because everybody is fighting something. It doesn’t matter where you’re from. Everybody gets tired, but everybody is still here,” he said. “When they hear this song, they’re going to say, ‘That’s me.’ And if it stops even one young person from giving up, then we did our job.”

Triple L also credits his upbringing in Trench Town, a community synonymous with reggae’s history, as an important part of the perspective he brings to his production.

“I didn’t come from comfort. I came from the concrete jungle, from Trench Town, the home of reggae music,” he said.

While some producers may focus on following the latest sounds, Triple L said his priority is authenticity.

“A lot of producers are chasing trends. I’m chasing truth. I take my pain, I don’t complain, and I turn it into music. And I’m not doing it for fame. I’m doing it for the youth who need to know that they’re worth more,” he said.

World.title: Restrepo wants more opportunities for developing athletes
World.content:
Jamaica’s Shanoya Douglas (left) and Trinidad and Tobago’s Kayla Charles compete in the Under-20 Girls’ 200m heat during the Carifta Games at Kirani James Stadium in St George’s, Grenada, on Sunday, April 5. (Photo: Dennis Allen for @TTGameplan)

WORLD Athletics presidential hopeful Ximena Restrepo says providing consistent, high-level competition for athletes who are not yet at the top level of track and field should be a priority for the next Administration of the global governing body.

Restrepo, the first woman to serve as a vice-president of World Athletics and its current senior vice-president, was in attendance at the recent World Under-20 Championships in Eugene, Oregon. She believes more can and should be done for athletes who do not have the resources to compete at top-level meets, most of which are staged in Europe.

The candidate, who is seeking to replace incumbent Sebastian Coe, believes a circuit that includes venues across the North American, Central American and Caribbean Athletic Association (NACAC) and South American regions would benefit athletes from those areas.

Restrepo, who attended the Carifta Games for the first time this year and was impressed with what she saw, said there are plenty of opportunities for junior athletes but questioned what happens after they leave school.

“There are competitions for the juniors. What happens with the seniors? What happens when the kids get out of school? That’s when things get tricky and not only on the islands; it happens all over the world,” she told the Jamaica Observer.

Not every athlete who signs their first professional contract will be able to get into the more prestigious meets. While there will be local competition, Restrepo said more needs to be done to keep those athletes in the sport.

“That’s when we really need to find out how to keep those kids in the sport. What do we offer them?” she said.
