“The prosecution also requested documents relating to the alleged handover of the bribe,” she added.

The prosecutor said the case contains direct evidence supported by other materials, and that there are no objective grounds to question its credibility.

Berdzenishvili said the defence argument that no third parties were present when the money changed hands was not significant to the case. According to her, demands for and payments of bribes generally do not take place in public or in the presence of large numbers of people.

Asked whether Mikautadze went directly to the SSS and handed the money to Liluashvili, Berdzenishvili replied: “Yes. According to the witness, that is what happened.”

The prosecutor said the investigation had also questioned other people who had previously visited Liluashvili. According to their testimony, the procedure for receiving visitors was not always the same.

“The witness also described how he entered the relevant office after undergoing a security check and other procedures. Other people who had previously visited Grigol Liluashvili were also questioned about how they entered the building. Security staff recorded the entry procedure and noted that it did not always involve issuing a pass, a search and so on. In other words, the defendant himself decided how visitors would enter his office,” Berdzenishvili said.

According to her, these circumstances and other factual evidence in the case support the reliability of the information Mikautadze provided to the court.

Berdzenishvili said Mikautadze told the businessmen that the money was being handed over in the interests of the state. According to the prosecutor, one of the businessmen also confirmed this.

“According to the witness, he told the businessmen that this was being done in the interests of the state. One of the businessmen also confirmed this during questioning. They presented the payment as something that served the state’s interests, although this was merely a formal justification. Of course, it was clear to everyone involved that it did not actually serve any state interest,” the prosecutor said.

Berdzenishvili also confirmed that, according to the investigation, Mikautadze brought the money to Liluashvili’s office in a bag.

“Yes, he had the money in his bag. As for his presence in the building, we questioned a security guard who confirmed that he saw Romeo Mikautadze, for example, on the same floor,” she said.

Journalists also asked the prosecutor whether Romeo Mikautadze could face charges, since he was the person who delivered the money to Liluashvili.

According to Berdzenishvili, the involvement of many people in the case is clear. However, authorities cannot classify a person’s actions as a crime until they launch criminal proceedings against that individual.

“I cannot call it a crime in advance until criminal proceedings have been launched against a particular person. I cannot classify a specific action as a crime — even in the case of Grigol Liluashvili. I am speaking based on the standard of reasonable suspicion. In general, if the case confirms that standard, criminal proceedings may be launched,” she said.

As for Mikautadze providing information to investigators, the prosecutor described it as cooperation. She said the defence was wrong to argue that Mikautadze was cooperating with investigators only to receive certain benefits and that such cooperation itself constituted a crime.

The prosecutor also did not rule out bringing criminal charges against Romeo Mikautadze in the future if investigators find sufficient grounds to do so.

“I did not rule that out. I simply described the situation that the defence presents as some kind of special case. I want to stress that the authorities will address the actions of all those involved, the decisions they made and the extent of their cooperation with the investigation within the framework of the law and justice,” Mariam Berdzenishvili said.

Background

Romeo Mikautadze is a former deputy economy minister. The State Security Service arrested him on 21 June 2025. According to the agency, Mikautadze faced charges of abuse of office and laundering millions of lari in illicit proceeds.

The case initially focused on corruption allegations against Mikautadze. In March 2026, a court sentenced him to 10 years in prison. Mikautadze also testified as a witness in the case against Grigol Liluashvili. The prosecution considers his testimony one of its key pieces of evidence.

Grigol Liluashvili headed the State Security Service from 2019 until April 2025. He left his post on 2 April 2025.

Liluashvili was arrested on 23 December 2025 after appearing for questioning at the prosecutor’s office. Investigators accuse him of receiving a particularly large bribe as part of a group acting in a prior agreement. According to the case file, the charges involve several episodes, including two linked to Romeo Mikautadze.

The charges against Liluashvili concern receiving a particularly large bribe. The relevant article carries a prison sentence of 11 to 15 years.

Corruption cases in Georgia

World.title: School uniforms return to Georgia’s public schools: what you need to know
World.content:
School uniforms in Georgia

Boys will wear jackets like these to school. Photo: Educational Resources

From the new school year, school uniforms will become compulsory for pupils from first to sixth grade in Georgia’s public schools. Boys will wear dark blue trousers and jackets, while girls will wear jackets made from the same material and skirts. The uniforms were made in China and consist mainly of synthetic materials.

The Education Ministry spent more than 45 million lari on the uniforms (approximately $17,226,540,000 — JAMnews). However, the uniforms will not be free for pupils, as parents will have to buy them from the government. Only children from socially vulnerable families will receive free sets.

The ministry says standardised uniforms will reduce social differences and strengthen pupils’ sense of belonging to their schools. However, some parents question the need for compulsory school uniforms. Their main concern is whether it makes sense to prioritise uniforms when more pressing problems with school infrastructure, safety and food remain unresolved.

Questions have also been raised about the quality and comfort of the uniforms. How comfortable will they be for young children? Will they be able to fasten the buttons and zips themselves? Will they be too hot in summer or too cold in winter?

Why has the school uniform become compulsory? How safe is the fabric used to make it for children’s health? Why did the government choose a Chinese company when Georgia also has a developed textile industry? What exactly will standardised uniforms change in Georgia’s troubled education system?

Why has the ministry decided to bring back school uniforms?

In September, six-year-old Ilia will begin a new stage of his life — he is starting school. Ilia attended kindergarten, but adapting to a new environment and stricter discipline will still be a challenge for him.

Ilia will face another challenge — running and playing during breaks in a polyester jacket and tight-fitting trousers.

“My son is used to wearing clothes made of cotton or wool with a small amount of elastane. Until he was six, he did not even wear jeans because they were not stretchy enough. I do not know how he will be able to run around in this jacket during school activities. And I wonder whether it will even stay on him. I doubt that restrictive clothing, against the backdrop of the stress of adapting to school, will help a child develop a sense of belonging to school life,” says Ilia’s mother, Taya Maharashvili.

Taya plans to contact the Education Ministry and demand stronger justification for making school uniforms compulsory:

“I have never opposed introducing a dress code. I believe it is important to dress appropriately in educational and professional environments, and children should learn this from an early age. However, the uniform proposed by the ministry is unacceptable.”

Introducing school uniforms for pupils in the lower grades of public schools is one element of a planned large-scale education reform. Education Minister Givi Mikanadze announced the measure on 2 December 2025 during a presentation of the National Concept for General Education Reform.

“School uniforms will help create an environment focused on learning and foster a sense of belonging to the educational institution. They will also reduce visible differences in pupils’ socio-economic backgrounds,” Mikanadze said.

School uniforms were compulsory in Georgia in the past. In Soviet schools, pupils wore dark brown, black or blue uniforms with white aprons. In independent Georgia, only some private schools require uniforms, although parents there have also complained about the quality of the fabric.

Polyester, viscose and elastane — what materials are used to make the clothes?

School uniform design. Photo: Education Ministry

The appearance, colour and quality of the school uniforms were determined entirely by the state. The boys’ uniforms will be plain dark blue, while the girls’ uniforms will feature a checked pattern. The state emblem will appear on the left side of the jacket.

The uniforms are made mainly from synthetic materials: 72% polyester, 25% viscose and 3% elastane.

The jackets will also have polyester lining. According to ministry documents, only the skirts will have cotton lining.

The uniforms can be washed at 40°C and ironed at 110°C. Bleach is prohibited, as is ironing the emblem or dry-cleaning the garment.

The school uniform set will include a jacket and trousers for boys, and a jacket and skirt (or a jacket and trousers) for girls.

“First of all, this uniform is uncomfortable. It reminds me of a situation where a paediatric dietitian insists that a child eat vegetables, only for the child to spit them out. I have the feeling that the ministry employs people who have no idea what children and childhood are like,” Taya says.

One uniform set will cost 95 lari. Some pupils will receive it for free.

Trousers and skirts will cost 25 lari, while a jacket will cost 45 lari. A set may include a jacket and two pairs of trousers, or a jacket, trousers and a skirt. As a result, one school uniform will cost parents 95 lari.

Most parents say one set will not be enough for a child to wear throughout the week. Pupils will also need a white shirt or T-shirt under the uniform, which parents will have to buy separately.

Pupils from socially vulnerable families will receive uniforms free of charge. This applies to families registered in the Unified Database of Socially Vulnerable Persons with a rating score below 65,001.

Children in state care or foster families, as well as those living in family-type homes or shelters for children without parental care, will also receive uniforms free of charge.

Ukrainian pupils who have been living and studying in Georgia since the start of the war will also receive school uniforms free of charge.

Is the uniform fabric safe? What should parents do if their child has an allergy or skin condition?

Third-grader Sandro has urticaria and allergic dermatitis. That is why his mother, Sopho, who is raising him alone, pays close attention to the quality of his clothes.

“My son is at school from 9:30am until 6pm, and I am concerned about everything: the quality, comfort and presence of allergens,” says Sopho Trapaidze.

Polyester, the material used for the uniforms, is widely used in the textile industry because it is durable and inexpensive. However, doctor Eka Kvirkvelia notes that the material is not suitable for everyone and is not hypoallergenic for all people. In some cases, it can contribute to overheating, increased sweating and skin irritation.

“True hypoallergenicity depends not only on the composition, but also on the fabric’s breathability, the chemical composition of dyes, production standards and the lining material. It is also important to understand that ‘international practice’ does not mean there is a single standard: different countries use different approaches. Nevertheless, natural fabrics or materials with a high cotton content are often preferred for primary school pupils,” she wrote on social media.

According to her, assessing the quality of school uniforms should rely on specific indicators, such as the percentage of each component, dermatological test results and data on children’s safety, rather than broad claims such as “hypoallergenic”.

Taya Maharashvili has also begun looking at practices in other countries. Polyester is used in schools in some developed countries, but there is one important detail:

“The percentage of polyester in our school uniforms is higher than in those countries. In addition, such countries more often introduce a dress code rather than a uniform. How the fabric has been treated and whether it meets safety standards are also important. They say these factors were taken into account when the Georgian school uniform was designed. However, the public should demand more reliable information supported by evidence, such as expert assessments and so on.”

Education Ministry says exceptions will be allowed

Parents are already demanding additional evidence from the Education Ministry that the fabric meets safety and quality standards. They are also calling on doctors to help address the issue.

“We demand a change in the fabric used for school uniforms. Synthetic clothing is harmful to children’s health,” Tamuna Gagnidze writes.

Dozens of parents have left comments under her post making similar demands. Many say they do not intend to dress their children in the uniforms.

“My child cannot wear polyester: he has atopic dermatitis, and contact with this material makes his skin worse. I absolutely do not want the school uniform to cause bleeding wounds on his skin,” says Hatuna Laghadze in a comment.

Sopho Trapaidze also does not plan to buy a new uniform for her son Sandro. She plans to make it herself — in the same style and colour, but from higher-quality material.

The Education Ministry says it will take into account cases where pupils have officially confirmed medical contraindications.

The Georgian Law on General Education regulates such cases. Article 19¹, paragraph 3, states that “a primary school pupil may be exempted from the obligation to wear a school uniform on health grounds based on a written agreement with the Ministry of Education”.

The ministry says such cases will be considered individually. Parents will need to provide the school with the relevant medical certificate. The pupil will still have to follow the established dress code.

What happens if a parent does not put their child in a school uniform?

School uniforms are compulsory. The ministry has placed particular emphasis on this point.

“Will they (officials — JAMnews) dress their own children in clothes made from this fabric?” This is the most common question in school groups and social media discussions about the uniforms.

“What happens if I do not put this uniform on my child? Will they be banned from going to school?” one parent asks in the comments.

“I have three school-age children. I am not going to buy it either. I consulted lawyers, and no one has the right to create problems for children because of this,” another parent replies.

When presenting the new uniforms, Education Minister Givi Mikanadze said that if parents refuse to use them, the school may address the issue through educational and disciplinary measures. The law does not specify which sanctions schools can impose.

The ministry says schools will consider each refusal on an individual basis. Each school will be able to find its own solution based on its internal rules.

What is known about the Chinese company making Georgia’s school uniforms?

School uniform production process. Photo: Educational Resources LLC

All matters related to the logistics of the school uniforms are handled by Educational Resources LLC, a department established within the Education Ministry in March 2026.

The ministry initially planned to manufacture the uniforms in Georgia. It considered using sewing workshops at state vocational colleges.

On 3 April 2026, the ministry announced a market study to procure the school uniforms. On 29 April, Educational Resources requested government approval to use a simplified procurement procedure. However, on 14 May, it emerged that the company initially selected did not meet the ministry’s requirements. The ministry had to restart the market study.

In June, the ministry signed a contract with Glory Textile Industry LLC to supply the school uniforms through direct negotiations, without a tender. The Education Ministry opted for direct negotiations to save time, as it needed to secure the uniforms and have them delivered before the start of the new school year.

Glory Textile Industry was registered in Georgia on 10 March 2026. Its sole owner and director is Chinese citizen Liu Xiaolin. The company received the order to manufacture the school uniforms just two months after its establishment and signed a 45.66 million lari contract with the Georgian government.

The company must deliver 1,801,000 items of clothing to Georgia between 25 August and 30 November:

Girls’ jackets — 292,000;

Boys’ jackets — 308,000;

Girls’ trousers — 438,000;

Boys’ trousers — 616,000;

Skirts — 146,000;

Long skirts — 1,000.

The uniforms are being made in China’s Jiangsu province at the Eton Kidd factory, which is operated by the SUMEC group.

Eton Kidd is a major Chinese school uniform brand. According to its official website, the company was founded in 2009. It works with more than 3,400 schools across 31 provincial-level administrative divisions, manufacturing and supplying school uniforms.

According to official information, SUMEC is an important subsidiary of the China National Machinery Industry Corporation (SINOMACH) and belongs to a group of state-owned enterprises directly under the central government of China.

Glory Textile Industry plans to deliver the school uniforms to Georgia in three stages:

Stage I — 301,000 items — by 25 August 2026;

Stage II — 600,000 items — by 15 October 2026;

Stage III — 900,000 items — by 30 November 2026.

First batch of uniforms arrives in Georgia. Where can parents get them?

The first batch of school uniforms has already arrived in Georgia. According to Educational Resources, the quantity is sufficient for first-graders.

The uniforms are currently being sorted into sets. Sales will begin on 1 September and continue until 14 September.

First batch of school uniforms. Photo: Educational Resources LLC

In the coming days, the uniforms will be distributed to major cities and regions. The authorities will also announce where parents can buy them. Parents will pay for the uniforms by cashless payment.

Uniforms for pupils in grades 2-6 will arrive later and will be distributed in two stages, on 15 October and 30 November.

This means pupils in grades 2-6 will not have uniforms in September. At the start of the school year, parents will have to buy regular clothes and purchase the uniforms later.

Will school uniforms change anything in Georgia’s education system?

The government is spending 45.66 million lari on school uniforms, saying they will help reduce social inequality. Meanwhile, Georgian schools still do not provide free meals.

According to a 2023 study by Georgia’s National Statistics Office, with support from UNICEF, only 27% of children aged 6 to 17 eat at school every day. Meanwhile, 34.9% do not eat at all during the school day. Among children from low-income families, the figure reaches 44.9%.

The same study found that 83.2% of parents believe schools should provide children with meals during the school day. In some Georgian schools, particularly in the regions, children cannot even buy food because the schools have no canteens.

Against the backdrop of these and other problems, school uniforms appear to be the least pressing issue facing Georgia’s public schools.

“I cannot support spending such a large amount of money on uniforms when schools have yet to address basic problems with toilets, canteens and the quality of education,” says Ana Gvaladze.

“We called the ministry 80 times to get the problem with the toilets at School No. 161 resolved,” adds Sopho Trapaidze.

Taya, who has been studying education issues in depth, says building a school culture is a complex process and involves much more than a set of behavioural rules:

“Schools face many problems today, from poor infrastructure and failures to meet health and hygiene standards to a lack of an emotionally safe environment for children. Children attend dull, grey schools. Sometimes a school has just one teacher, who provides the support that the education system as a whole should provide. So school culture cannot be strengthened through uniforms alone. Likewise, in such an unhealthy environment — and given the problems with crime in the country — uniforms cannot stop bullying.”

Taya notes that bullying does not actually start because of clothing.

“Clothing is just an excuse. If a bully is looking for a victim, they can pick on someone’s height, weight, glasses, shoes, bag or even pen. Uniforms cannot hide social differences. And most importantly, when the minister talked about school culture and a sense of belonging, did he forget that a child who is hungry because their school has no canteen will not develop any sense of belonging?”

Hundreds of thousands of Georgian schoolchildren will start the new academic year in “impoverished” conditions, in buildings that are not suitable for proper education. In recent years, hundreds of schools across the country have been demolished, while construction on many replacements has yet to begin.

School uniforms in Georgia

World.title: Former Georgian PM Irakli Garibashvili accuses Ivanishvili of blackmail
World.content:
Former PM accuses Ivanishvili of blackmail

Jailed former Georgian prime minister Irakli Garibashvili has accused Georgian Dream honorary chairman Bidzina Ivanishvili and the current government of blackmail.

In a statement released from prison on 17 August 2026, the former prime minister claimed he was being pressured to plead guilty to new corruption charges and permanently withdraw from politics at Ivanishvili’s demand. It is the first time that a former close ally of Ivanishvili has openly spoken out against the founder of the ruling party.

Plea deal ultimatum and plan to quit politics

A photograph of a printed letter dated 17 August was posted on the Facebook pages of Garibashvili and his wife, Nunuka Tamazashvili. Only four paragraphs of the letter were made public. It is unclear who wrote the letter or how it was delivered.

According to the published document, the government is offering the former prime minister a compromise. Under the proposed terms, Garibashvili would have to plead guilty to a new corruption-related charge.

The letter sets out the proposal in detail:

“They are offering me the option of pleading guilty in one case, where everything would be arranged by agreement, including a confession, witness signatures and so on. They are offering a plea bargain while retaining the same five-year sentence: that is, as it has been explained to me, the sentences would be combined, but the final term would remain five years.”

According to the document, a corruption conviction would serve as a form of “insurance” for the government, aimed at preventing the former prime minister from returning to politics in the future.

Two options and a political condition

The published letter refers to investigations into several cases. Its author suggests that these could result in corruption charges.

The text outlines two possible courses of action for Garibashvili. The first would involve continuing to contest the case in court.

“Let’s discuss this seriously and see it through to the end,” the document says.

The second option is presented as a compromise. According to the letter, Garibashvili would plead guilty in one of the cases, with the details agreed in advance:

“Let’s plead guilty in one case, where everything will be arranged by agreement: a confession, witness signatures and so on.”

The document also says that a new plea deal would not increase the five-year prison sentence already imposed on Garibashvili. The sentences would be combined, leaving the overall term unchanged at five years.

However, the proposal comes with a political condition.

“After leaving, you cannot engage in politics. If it is decided to ‘renege on the agreements’, then the corruption charges that will be brought will serve as an insurance mechanism, preventing even the thought of returning to politics,” the document says.

The authenticity of the letter has not been independently verified, and its author remains unknown. There is also no confirmation that new cases are in fact being prepared against Garibashvili.

Garibashvili’s first open confrontation with Ivanishvili

This marks Irakli Garibashvili’s first public confrontation with Bidzina Ivanishvili. For many years, Garibashvili was regarded as one of his most loyal political allies.

He served twice as Georgia’s prime minister, first from 2013 to 2015 and again from 2021 to 2024.

Garibashvili was sentenced under a plea agreement reached on 12 January 2026. He was given a five-year prison term and fined one million lari. Two cars and $6.5m were also confiscated from him.

The case concerned the laundering of illicit proceeds on an especially large scale. Garibashvili is currently serving his sentence in a prison in Rustavi.

The new statement means that the former prime minister himself is now linking possible further legal action against him to demands that he stay out of politics. However, the material made public so far presents only Garibashvili’s version of events.

Response from MP Irma Inashvili, named in letter

The letter published by Garibashvili mentions MP Irma Inashvili and Dito Chubinidze. According to the text, they — along with “supporters like them” and campaigns on social media — have raised suspicions.

“Supporters such as Dito Chubinidze and Irma Inashvili, as well as campaigns organised on social media, have raised very serious suspicions and caused us tangible harm,” the document says.

Inashvili denied any involvement in organised campaigns. She said Irakli Garibashvili was her friend, but that she expressed her views publicly and independently.

“I have never planned or conducted any campaigns on social media; I don’t need such campaigns — I already express my views openly in my own name!” Inashvili wrote.

She said Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze was the main target of her criticism.

“I expose Kobakhidze and fight against him,” Inashvili said.

Opposition says Garibashvili being politically neutralised

Opposition figures have described Garibashvili’s letter as a sign of an internal conflict within the government. Their comments amount to political assessments and do not independently corroborate the circumstances described in the letter.

Nika Gvaramia, one of the leaders of the Coalition for Change, said the contents of the letter pointed to a political motive behind Garibashvili’s imprisonment.

“Ivanishvili’s bargaining with Garibashvili — ‘I will punish you even more severely unless you give me guarantees that you will leave politics for good’ — confirms that the motive for his arrest is neither to punish a corrupt official nor to fight corruption in general, nor does it serve any public or state interest. It serves Bidzina’s personal political interests,” Gvaramia wrote.

He also qualified his comments by noting that the authenticity of the letter had not been established. Gvaramia particularly highlighted what he described as an attempt to politically neutralise Garibashvili.

Levan Samushia, a member of the Lelo – Strong Georgia party, linked the statement to the country’s current system of governance. He said any potential threat against Garibashvili’s family warranted a legal response.

“It is clear that Garibashvili is speaking about a possible, alleged threat to his family. This is an issue that requires particular attention and, naturally, provides grounds for launching an investigation,” Samushia said.

Berdia Sichinava, a representative of the Gakharia for Georgia party, said he preferred to wait for further information before reaching a definitive conclusion. Nevertheless, he linked the developments to an internal conflict within Georgian Dream.

“The situation appears alarming because it concerns his family, and at this point clarity is the best means of protecting him and his loved ones,” Sichinava said.

Khatia Dekanoidze, one of the leaders of the United National Movement, described Garibashvili’s case as a warning to current government figures.

“Garibashvili’s case should be learnt by heart by Ivanishvili’s current servants, officials and representatives of the financial sector who justify the government,” Dekanoidze wrote.

Government silent as questions remain unanswered

At the time of writing, reports about Garibashvili’s allegations had not appeared on the websites or Facebook pages of the pro-government Imedi and Rustavi 2 television channels.

Government representatives have yet to respond publicly to the central allegation. They have not said whether Bidzina Ivanishvili had any involvement in sending the letter to Garibashvili. It also remains unclear whether any new investigations into the former prime minister are under way.

Background: From alliance to prison

For many years, Irakli Garibashvili was regarded as one of Bidzina Ivanishvili’s closest political allies. He served twice as Georgia’s prime minister.

On 24 October 2025, Garibashvili was charged with laundering illicit proceeds on an especially large scale. A plea agreement was reached on 12 January 2026, under which the former prime minister was sentenced to five years in prison and fined one million lari. Two cars and $6.5m were also confiscated. He has since been serving his sentence at a penitentiary facility in Rustavi.

Legal proceedings against former senior figures in the ruling team were preceded by internal party disagreements and arrests of officials from various state agencies. There have also been reports of investigative measures involving members of Garibashvili’s family.

The developments suggest that the power struggle within Georgian Dream has entered an increasingly acute phase.

World.title: Why Seoul has called for peace talks to formally end the Korean War
World.content:
South Korea's leader wants to sit down with North Korea and make peace.

North and South Korea are technically still at war as the agreement made to stop fighting on the Korean Peninsula in 1953 was an armistice, not a peace treaty.

Now South Korea has once again called for talks to formally end the Korean War.

So how significant is Seoul's offer and what could it mean for peace on the Korean Peninsula?

North and South Korea are technically still at war. (AFP: Roger-Viollet)

A wide breach to cross

Attempts have been made from both sides to formally end the war over the years, with sticking points including the US military presence in the South and more recently North Korea's nuclear program.

Since taking office last year, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung's administration has taken a more conciliatory approach than his hawkish predecessor impeached president Yoon Suk Yeol.

Yoon was sentenced to life in prison earlier this year on charges of rebellion over his attempt to put the country under military rule.

Jay Song, an associate professor from Australian National University, said the centre-left Lee government had a pro-engagement peace policy and had not given up on unification "one day".

"Ending the war first, peace building next and finally if conditions are met, try one Korea," she said.

On the other side of the demilitarised zone, North Korea has abandoned its official aim of unification in recent years, with leader Kim Jong Un declaring South Korea as the North's "most hostile state".

In 2024, the authoritarian dictatorship said it would permanently block its border with South Korea and boost its front-line defence posture to cope with "confrontational hysteria" by South Korean and US forces.

"The important thing here is that the nature of the inter-Korean relations remains hostile so that Pyongyang can continue to develop its nuclear weapons and missiles," Dr Song said.

North Korea expert Leonid Petrov said nuclear weapons were a non-negotiable for the North as they served as a guarantee of regime survival.

"Any contact, exchange, or cooperation with South Korea poses serious security risks to the North Korean political system because such engagement undermines its legitimacy and its myths of superiority," said Dr Petrov, who teaches Korean studies at the Australian National University.

Korean Liberation Day is celebrated in both the North and the South. (Reuters: Lee Jin-man)

How significant was the speech?

Mr Lee extended the most recent olive branch during a speech on Saturday to mark Korea's liberation from Japanese colonial rule.

Liberation Day is celebrated by both North and South Korea, though with diverging narratives.

"Let us put down our intentions to threaten each other and begin discussions to end the long-running war as the directly involved parties," Mr Lee said.

"Through this, it may also be possible to discuss effective measures to halt the advancement of North Korea's nuclear capabilities," he added.

Dr Song pointed out that without a formal peace treaty war could resume at any time.

Ministers tread carefully as Trump scales back drills Australia and Japan's defence ministers discuss the rapidly expanding defence ties between the two countries.

"In fact, there have been many clashes and skirmishes at the land and maritime borders," she said.

"People living on the Korean Peninsula have internalised this unstable conflict situation for more than 70 years.

"Mistrust, surveillance and violence have been normalised.

"In this context, President Lee's call for ending the war and establishing a peace regime is significant."

Alexander Hynd, a lecturer at the University of Melbourne's Asia Institute, said some people saw the peace treaty talks as "unfinished business".

"For others, this is low-hanging fruit that can be helpful in kickstarting more meaningful inter-Korean talks and future cooperation," he said.

"North Korea has so far largely ignored South Korean President Lee's attempts to improve relations since he was elected last June," he added.

'We can achieve peace'

For some members of Australia's Korean diaspora, Mr Lee's calls for peace talks has been decades in the making.

Sun Jung from Werribee in Melbourne said she was "delighted" when she heard.

"This approach has been lacking for so many years," Ms Jung told the ABC.

" I really believe that through dialogue and communication, we can achieve peace. "

Sun Jung was "delighted" when she heard about Lee Jae Myung's speech. (ABC News: Angelica Silva)

Ms Jung said her family carries the war inside them. Her father was around 15 years old when it began — his brothers and his parents were affected too.

"They all went through the war. They suffered," she said.

"They've seen it all, from poverty to ashes from all the burning.

"People there have suffered enough."

But while Ms Jung welcomed the prospect of peace talks, she said a treaty was only the first step.

"To me, peace is not just about the absence of war or a formal paper that needs to be signed," she said.

"It is about respecting human life and every individual's right to live."

Ms Jung, who became a citizen in 2005, has lived in Australia longer than she has in South Korea.

While she said that she does not follow Korean current events "all the time", moments like Mr Lee's comments pull her back in.

"In my blood and in my heart is Korea," she said.

"So, I like to know what's happening there, and I want to contribute in any way."

North Korea has "permanently" shut its border with South Korea. (AP: Lee Jin-man)

A bid to restart diplomacy

Jenny Town, senior fellow and director of 38 North at the Stimson Center, told the ABC's The World South Korea had long been trying to figure out how to restart diplomacy with North Korea.

The North's decision to label South Korea a permanent hostile state meant the political infrastructure that had allowed negotiations had been severed.

"They keep trying to find ways to rebuild this relationship, knowing that they need to lower tensions … they don't want this constant pressure and tension," she said.

"With the Liberation Day speech, I think this was their way of saying that they don't have to be in a permanently hostile arrangement with each other."

Nonetheless, Dr Town said there still was not a consensus in South Korea on formally ending the war because it had become so tied to the relationship with the US.

"If you see the war as a function of maintaining the alliance, then the status quo is preferable over severing the alliance as a whole," she said.

"But technically the alliance is not contingent on the war continuing. It is a separate agreement … and should be dealt with separately than the actual formal ending of the war itself."

Donald Trump says he and Kim Jong Un understand each other. (AP: Susan Walsh)

Could peace talks actually go ahead?

North Korea has yet to officially respond to Mr Lee's outreach.

Complicating matters, North Korea has in recent times formed increasingly close ties with Russia while the United States under President Donald Trump has been sowing doubt about his commitment to supporting South Korea.

Dr Petrov said Mr Lee's proposal was "falling on deaf ears" because Mr Kim had a better deal with Russia.

"These days, Moscow is offering cash, energy, and advanced military technology — effectively making international sanctions irrelevant — in exchange for North Korean troops and conventional weapons to be used against Ukraine," he said.

US allies question Washington's reliability President Donald Trump's late call to "substantially reduce" military exercises with South Korea has prompted speculation he is courting a meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

On Sunday, Mr Trump ordered the Pentagon to scale back planned joint military exercises with South Korea, saying it declined to help denuclearise Iran and citing his good relationship with Mr Kim.

The US on Tuesday local time confirmed the exercises would conclude on August 21, a week earlier than scheduled.

Dr Hynd said he did not view Mr Lee's offer as likely to lead to a major breakthrough in inter-Korean relations.

"If anything, it is more about steadying the ship and locking in the status quo, at a time when President Lee's major challenge is how to deal with President Trump's unpredictability and general ambivalence towards the US-South Korea alliance."

Dr Song said peace was not easy to achieve on the Korean Peninsula.

"It's not just the two Koreas' problem but intertwined with great powers around them: the US, China, Russia and Japan," she said.

"It appears the only party that desperately wants peace is South Korea at the moment.

"The others all want a flashpoint in that region to grow their own power and influence."

Additional reporting by Girish Sawlani

World.title: UK's new PM messaged with person claiming to be Trump's chief of staff
World.content:
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has confirmed he exchanged messages with someone pretending to be US President Donald Trump's chief of staff.

Speaking to reporters during a visit to central England on Tuesday, Mr Burnham said he was not embarrassed by the incident, which was raised with the White House.

Here's what to know.

What happened?

Politico first reported on Monday that Mr Burnham engaged with "a few messages" sent by someone impersonating White House chief of staff Susie Wiles via an unspecified communication channel.

Mr Burnham said he became suspicious of the contact and reported the incident.

The British embassy in Washington then raised the matter with the White House, according to two sources cited by Politico.

The White House did not immediately respond to an ABC request for comment.

Andy Burnham with West Midlands Mayor Richard Parker during his visit to Wolverhampton Bus Station on Tuesday. (Reuters: Hannah McKay/Pool)

What was said in the messages?

We don't have the details.

The messages have not been released to the public, and Downing Street has declined to say when the exchange occurred or how many messages were sent.

But Mr Burnham has said nothing sensitive had been discussed during the "minimal exchange".

"Nothing of consequence, and actually, quickly I realised that this needed to be reported, and I did so," he said during a visit to the central English city of Wolverhampton.

Have there been security incidents like this before?

Yes.

Federal authorities began investigating a similar effort to impersonate Ms Wiles in 2025, according to reports published in May of that year.

The FBI probe came after an unknown individual who posed as Ms Wiles contacted prominent Republicans and business executives.

Susie Wiles told associates last year that her phone had been hacked. (Reuters: Daniel Heuer)

Ms Wiles told associates her personal phone had been hacked and the information on her contact list exposed.

Several people who received messages from the person claiming to be Ms Wiles reportedly became suspicious when the impersonator attempted to move the conversations to Telegram.

Mr Burnham is not the first British leader to fall victim to a hoax call, either.

Boris Johnson gaffe Britain's Foreign Secretary Boris Johnson talks international relations and rude poetry with a hoax caller.

Boris Johnson talked about sanctions against Russia during a hoax call that lasted 18 minutes while he was foreign secretary in 2018.

And former prime minister David Cameron fell victim to hoaxes in 2024 and 2015.

In the more recent incident, he spoke with someone impersonating former Ukrainian president Petro Poroshenko via a call and text messages.

While he was prime minister in 2015, Downing Street connected him with a caller pretending to be the head of the UK Government Communications Headquarters.

How has Burnham responded?

Asked on Tuesday, local time, whether he was embarrassed at being taken in, Mr Burnham said: "No, I'm not."

"I handled it in the right way. All politicians are receiving these pressures and these challenges, but I did everything right," he said.

He added that the "correct action" was taken in both the UK and US.

How can you spot a scam caller?

While this hoax call may have been tailored to Mr Burnham, scammers can target anyone.

Here are some quick warning signs that a caller may be a scammer, according to Scamwatch:

They ask for personal or financial information: payment, or for you to move money between accounts your password, PIN, one-time code, or some other security information credit card or banking details to process a refund or other "overpayment"

They want you to install software or access a secure account on your mobile phone or computer

They threaten you with immediate arrest, deportation, or blackmail

They suggest you or your accounts have been hacked or involved in fraud

They tell you about a way to make quick, easy money with little risk or effort.

ABC/AFP

World.title: South Australian couple missing in Tasmania
World.content:
Tasmania Police has deployed search and rescue teams in the state's north-west after an elderly couple visiting from South Australia was reported missing.

Clementina, 81, and her 79-year-old partner Peter were last seen at 2:30pm yesterday in Milabena, 44 kilometres west of Burnie, in Tasmania's north.

The couple was visiting family in Tasmania and had embarked on an afternoon of sightseeing, with their destination unknown.

Peter, pictured in an image released by police. (Supplied: Tasmania Police)

Police believe they may be with their vehicle, a silver Honda CR-V with South Australian registration S744ACB.

Police believe the pair may have intended to travel to the Penguin, Gawler and Gunns Plains area.

The couple was first reported missing last night after they did not return home as planned and their family were unable to get in contact with them.

The silver 2008 Honda CRV driven by the South Australian couple in Tasmania. (Supplied: Tasmania Police)

Unfavourable weather marring search

Clementina is described as about 149 centimetres tall, of solid build and was last seen wearing a green sherpa-lined hoodie, blue or black pants and black lace-up shoes.

Peter is described as of solid build, with grey hair, glasses, no facial hair and about 170 cm tall.

He was wearing a navy blue hoodie, navy blue track pants and New Balance sneakers when last seen by family members.

The police helicopter has been requested to aid the search, but unfavourable weather conditions in the area have prevented it from assisting so far.

Anyone with information or who may have seen the couple or their silver car is being urged to contact Tasmania Police on 131 444.

World.title: Academic abused for support of Jewish Australians, royal commission told
World.content:
Prominent academic and advocate for Indigenous Australians Marcia Langton says she has been subjected to abuse and labelled a "zio" by members of the pro-Palestinian movement.

Dr Langton appeared before the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion on Wednesday to discuss the role of education in tackling all forms of racism and hate, including antisemitism.

She said she had been subjected to racism and abuse because of her support for Jewish Australians.

"I've been labelled a zio by the pro-Palestine movement in Melbourne. I've had people pull out of panels that I was listed to speak at … my car's windows were smashed," she said.

"Labelling me as a zio … I'm therefore made voiceless in the debate.

"Because as much as I might be horrified and oppose what's happening in Gaza … the foul treatment of Jewish Australians cannot be justified by saying that Israel is doing this in Gaza."

Childcare fostering social cohesion

The commission also heard from a Jewish Australian woman working to foster social cohesion in her childcare centre, which has about 70 per cent non-Jewish families on its books.

Known as AEA, the woman said the centre introduces children to Jewish culture by creating sensory experiences influenced by tradition.

She said the aim of this was to celebrate difference, while also highlighting the values and experiences children of different cultures share with their friends.

"There is no intention for a non-Jewish child to adopt that practice … but what it is is connecting on those shared values," she said.

For example, AEA said each Friday children participate in challah baking, with the loaves of bread taken home to be shared with family.

"This is a very distinct tradition … but the values underneath that is something we all share. That idea of sharing food with family," she said.

AEA said work was underway to develop a pilot program based on the centre's model.

World.title: Before and after photos show impact of SpaceX rocket that slammed into Moon
World.content:
A NASA spacecraft circling the Moon is providing the sharpest views yet of a crater carved by a crashing SpaceX rocket, with the space agency releasing before-and-after photos of the impact area.

The SpaceX Falcon rocket's upper stage ploughed into the Moon at 8,700 kilometres per hour on August 5 after drifting through space for more than a year.

SpaceX's Falcon 9 rocket lifted off on March 14, 2025, carrying NASA's Crew-10 astronauts to the International Space Station. (Reuters: Joe Skipper)

Between August 11 and August 12, NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter captured a series of images of the new crater.

Based on these new photos, the fresh crater appears to be 18 metres across and less than 3m deep, according to scientists, who NASA said determined the measurements based on the length of the crater's shadow.

Rocket Moon crash Part of a SpaceX rocket has crashed into the Moon, with the impact likely to be seen from Earth.

Dark and bright streaks are clearly visible emanating like butterfly wings from the crater.

The darker lines represent excavated material that was close to the surface and shaped by eons of solar wind, cosmic rays and micro-meteorite strikes.

The brighter rays indicate fresh rocks and dirt that were hurled from farther down.

The spacecraft photographed the crater a week after the collision from 96km up, while zooming along at 1.6km per second.

An animation from the Solar System Registry shows the moment a remnant of the Falcon 9 rocket crashes into the Moon. (Supplied: Solar System Registry)

Flight controllers had to tilt the spacecraft so its cameras pointed toward the impact scene.

NASA said the spacecraft was required to "wait until that location turn[ed] into view, which took six days in this case".

The orbiter completes a lunar polar orbit every two hours as the Moon rotates beneath.

South Korea's Danuri spacecraft was first on the scene to beam back photos.

The Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter has been orbiting the Moon since 2009, serving as NASA's up-close eyes as the space agency works to return astronauts to the lunar surface.

AP

World.title: 'Liar loans' leave property market open to criminal exploitation
World.content:
Hundreds of millions of dollars of suspected fraudulent loans have been uncovered at 10 major banks during an operation involving Australia's top-tier financial regulation and criminal intelligence agencies.

Operation Claw has exposed coordinated mortgage fraud and "systemic weaknesses" across the lending sector, with properties, mainly in Sydney, being bought in a way that does not comply with laws meant to ensure responsible lending and cut down on dirty cash.

"The scale of this activity should be a wake-up call for every lender," AUSTRAC chief executive Brendan Thomas said.

"The same warning signs were found across banks that together cover the vast majority of Australia's mortgage market.

"While this project did not identify evidence of widespread money laundering, the weaknesses it exposed could be exploited by criminals seeking to abuse Australia's financial system."

Brendan Thomas says the revelations should act as a "wake-up call" for lenders. (ABC News: John Gunn)

The banking industry said it welcomed the action by the financial crimes agency and would continue to work with law enforcement and regulators to stamp down on suspected fraud.

"This work has included intelligence sharing between banks and AUSTRAC through the Fintel Alliance, which has already proven effective in uncovering fraudulent loan activity," Australian Banking Association chief executive Simon Birmingham said.

Simon Birmingham says the banking industry needs access to ATO income data. (AAP: Lukas Coch)

Mr Birmingham said banks would continue to advocate for secure access to income data from the Australian Taxation Office (ATO) to help reduce the use of fraudulent loan documents.

"Verified ATO data would give lenders a single, trusted source of truth for a customer’s income and be a new tool banks could deploy to prevent loan fraud into the future," he said.

Years of 'liar loan' warnings

The money has been lent out in what are called "liar loans".

AUSTRAC described the suspected fraud as using the following to support loan applications:

inflated incomes

misrepresented employment

fabricated or unverifiable business activity

There were also cases in which "offshore or third-party funds" were used to finalise settlements and make mortgage repayments.

The agency said this demonstrated how false income streams and complex funding arrangements can wash money through the Australian property market.

What a 20pc property downturn looks like Canada and New Zealand have never recovered from their pre-COVID property market records. It is worthwhile examining what we can learn.

It is not a new issue.

In recent years, investment bank UBS asked borrowers about their honesty when filling out applications. In 2021 its survey of about 900 people showed 41 per cent submitted loan applications that were not completely factually accurate.

The most common areas of inaccuracy were under-representing living costs (34 per cent), under-representing financial commitments (28 per cent) and over-representing income (22 per cent).

Borrowers who used mortgage brokers were far more likely to submit inaccurate applications (44 per cent) versus those who applied directly through a bank (29 per cent).

Last year corporate regulator ASIC sued the Westpac-owned RAMS for systemic misconduct in arranging loans, including fake payslips being submitted for mortgage applications, and customers' debts and expenses being altered so they would meet loan serviceability requirements.

In October, the Federal Court ordered RAMS to pay a $20 million penalty after admitting to "widespread compliance failures". This month RAMS's book of home loans was sold to Pepper Money for $15.4 billion.

'Operation Claw' goes wide

People involved in submitting fake documents that support loan applications might be getting a knock on the door.

Mr Thomas said Operation Claw had already made referrals to appropriate authorities.

Operation Claw involved AUSTRAC working closely with banks, the ATO, NSW Police, the NSW Crime Commission, the Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission and financial regulators APRA and ASIC.

ABC Business Daily The podcast that helps you unpack the latest business and finance news.

"Every lender should be looking closely at these findings and asking whether the same vulnerabilities exist in their own business," Mr Thomas said.

"The most effective way to stop mortgage fraud is before a loan is approved.

"Once a loan is established and the funds have moved, recovering the money becomes significantly harder.

"Lenders need to actively look for these warning signs, strengthen their controls and report suspicious activity to AUSTRAC. This is not something any institution can afford to ignore."

World.title: Days of downpour threaten outback music festival as gates remain closed
World.content:
Several days of rain in far west New South Wales is threatening one of Australia's largest outback music festivals.

Organisers of the Mundi Mundi Bash, roughly 40 kilometres north-west of Broken Hill, are deciding whether to go ahead with the event.

The wet weather has hampered the roll-in of vehicles over the past few days, with some lining up overnight to enter the grounds.

Wilangee Road, used to access the festival, is now closed to all vehicles except four-wheel-drives.

The Mundi Mundi Bash site is partially flooded following widespread rain. (Supplied: Peter Nash)

Monique McGrath is attending her first Mundi Mundi Bash with a group of 14 friends, who have travelled from Dubbo, Illawarra and Port Macquarie.

She said they began lining up to enter the festival site at about 1pm yesterday, but were not granted access until this morning.

"It was very slow … we camped in the line-up," Ms McGrath said.

"I took photos [of the line-up of caravans] and it just went for miles and miles and miles."

She said the conditions had been less than favourable.

"Very muddy, the rain last night was absolutely horrendous," Ms McGrath said.

"We've actually got one of our crew members bogged at the moment, so we're just waiting on a recovery vehicle to come out and pull these guys out."

Wilangee Road, used to access the festival site is now closed to all vehicles except four-wheel-drives. (ABC Broken Hill: Oliver Brown)

Mary and Graham travelled from Adelaide with a group of six caravans to attend Mundi, and reported lining up for more than four hours.

"All the roadways, which [when] we were here two years ago were lovely and dry, are [now] just muddy messes," Mary said.

"We managed to all get in and none of us got bogged, but people around us are bogged.

"[Some people] had to camp on the roadways, within the camp, but there's also people [who] camped on the external roadway because they shut the gates and had nowhere to go.

"This morning, they're all moving quite slowly."

For Lincoln Dalla Santa from Mildura, who has attended every Mundi Bash, the crazy weather is simply part of the outback experience.

Lincoln Dalla Santa (right) says the crazy weather is all part of the outback experience. (ABC Broken Hill: Bill Ormonde)

"[The weather] doesn't really faze me, whether it's muddy, whether it's hot, it doesn't matter, it's just part of what it is," Mr Dalla Santa said.

"You wouldn't have an outback festival if it wasn't [braving] the elements.

" What nature dishes out, we just gotta live with that. "

Organisers have said they will provide an update at 2pm today.

More rain on the way

A total of 11.6 millimetres of rain was recorded by the Bureau of Meteorology at the Broken Hill Airport over Monday and Tuesday.

Forecasts from the bureau show more rain and a possible storm is on the cards for the region tonight and tomorrow.

Senior meteorologist Angus Hines said the rain was quite uncommon for winter in the region.

"[It is] pretty dry normally at this time of year as we push through the cooler months," he said.

" The average in Broken Hill for August rainfall is about 18 millimetres, but we've had already two pretty solid dumps of rain just in the past couple of weeks, which have well and truly exceeded that monthly average. "

Mr Hines said the wet weather system was not done yet, with more showers and possible storms expected overnight and tomorrow.

"If the storms do get going then we could see some locally moderate, or even heavy rainfall with those storms directly overhead," he said.

Police are only allowing limited access to the road out of Broken Hill towards the festival site. (ABC Broken Hill: Bill Ormonde)

Thunderstorms would bring the lion's share of the rain, but even if they do not occur, wet weather is guaranteed.

"We could really see anything from a couple of millimetres tonight, perhaps 2, 3 or 5mm, or if we get some heavier showers and storms moving through, we might well see something like 10 or 15mm," Mr Hines said

World.title: Man who shot victim in face for being intimate with girlfriend jailed
World.content:
A man who shot a drug dealer because he had been intimate with his girlfriend has been jailed for more than two years by the ACT Supreme Court.

The court heard Bradley John Wilson wanted to "exact retribution" on the victim when he used a home-made shotgun to shoot him at close range in March last year, seriously injuring his face and shoulder.

Wilson's then-girlfriend had lured the victim to the home in Lyneham in Canberra's north under the pretence of buying drugs from him, the court heard.

The attack happened on the same day Wilson was released from custody in relation to other matters.

The court heard that Wilson held a belief that the victim had been intimate with his girlfriend while he was imprisoned and was motivated to "exact retribution."

Offender suffering from 'profound grief disorder'

Wilson, 26, has been on remand since the incident occurred.

He pleaded guilty to two offences, including discharging a firearm and joint commission of assault occasioning actual bodily harm, with the court also considering a less serious charge of unlawful possession of a firearm.

Justice Andrew Muller said Wilson's offending and his prior anti-social behaviour were closely linked to the "extreme and profound" impact of the death of Wilson's mother when he was a child.

The court heard the 26-year-old was suffering from "prolonged grief disorder" after his mother was killed in a car driven by Wilson's father, who had swerved to avoid a kangaroo.

He had helped remove his mother from the wreckage, Justice Muller said, which marked the onset of his substance abuse, including a "pathological" pattern of behaviour associated with his amphetamine and cannabis use.

The judge said he accepted Wilson's letter of apology and expression of genuine remorse, despite scepticism from prosecutors about whether he was genuine.

Wilson was sentenced to two years and nine months' in jail for the three offences, with a non-parole period of one year and six months.

But because Wilson's offending occurred while he was subject to two separate good behaviour orders for unrelated offending, an additional six months was added to his sentence.

Wilson will be eligible for parole from March 2027, accounting for the time he has already served.

World.title: McRae did not read the AFL memo, but admits having sleepless nights over resting players
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 McRae did not read the AFL memo, but admits having sleepless nights over resting players Danny Russell August 19, 2026 — 2:07pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Collingwood will bring back veterans Jeremy Howe and Steele Sidebottom for Friday night’s clash with Brisbane, but coach Craig McRae remains guarded over whether the club will rest tired players ahead of their looming sudden-death wildcard final. McRae said Brayden Maynard (leg) failed a fitness test and would not play against the Lions at the MCG, while Isaac Quaynor (glute) will be another omission from the team that drew with Hawthorn last round. Collingwood coach Craig McRae will welcome back Jeremy Howe, centre, but Brayden Maynard will miss again. AFL Photos via Getty Images But the Collingwood coach declined to comment on whether the Magpies would manage individual players, such as Nick and Josh Daicos, for their final home-and-away match. The Magpies, who announced an AFL record of 113,362 members on Wednesday, are sitting eighth with potential to move to seventh, while Brisbane need to win to avoid dropping from third to outside the top four.



“I’ve heard the narrative, everyone’s trying to take us towards the Bulldogs (ninth), which is a potential (wildcard) match-up, but it could be Carlton (10th), it could be anyone else,” McRae said on Wednesday ahead of their match committee meeting. Related Article Money Talks

AFL 2026 Why Clarkson is leading North’s push to woo this rival defender “Everyone’s trying to take us to towards the future, and we’re really just determined to stay here, what’s relevant right now, and control what we can around that.” McRae said his playing group and club were “really hungry” to take momentum and rhythm into a new-look finals series. “No one’s had this in the history of a game – in this format, anyway. So we’ll learn some lessons along the way,” he said.



“There’s no perfect answer to it. We rest five players, we’ll be judged on that. We don’t rest five players, we will be judged on that. “I’d be lying if I said I hadn’t had sleepless nights thinking about all the scenarios around what could be and what may be, but the reality is that we’ll just deal in what we can control. Steele Sidebottom will retire at the end of this year. Getty Images “And, I’ll repeat, there’s an appetite to keep playing. All our players are really hungry to keep performing really well.” McRae said Collingwood’s selection process would not be affected by an AFL memo earlier this month that warned clubs they would be fined if they rested players en masse.



“They set parameters in place for a reason because they want the integrity of the game to be in place,” McRae said. “But management of players is delicate. There’s so many layers to it. There’s training, there’s playing, there’s all sorts of things that we have the data around, and we’ll make the appropriate decisions regarding all that. “I didn’t read it [the memo]. I know [Collingwood football manager] Charlie Gardiner read it and articulated that to us, and I think it’s a bit of a common-sense thing that they don’t want 15 players rested. But, again, we’ll do what’s best for what we think we need for this weekend and beyond.” McRae said he understood the ongoing interest from rival clubs in games record-holder Scott Pendlebury, but could not imagine a future in which he was not at Collingwood next year.

World.title: WiseTech raided by competition watchdog, smashing shares
World.content:
The competition watchdog has raided WiseTech Global, in another blow to the logistics software company, sending its shares plummeting.

WiseTech told the ASX on Wednesday that an Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) search warrant had been executed on the company as part of an investigation into alleged breaches of competition law, requiring it to produce documents and electronic data relating to the supply of global logistics services and software. The company said it intended to fully cooperate. Its shares fell about 11 per cent to $38.58.

WiseTech founder Richard White. Dominic Lorrimer

WiseTech has been embroiled in controversy over the past two years, and this action is the first by a regulator aimed squarely at the company rather than at billionaire founder Richard White personally. The Australian Federal Police is investigating White over allegations first reported by this masthead that he coerced a former WiseTech cleaner into a sexual relationship and provided false information to secure her a visa, claims he denies.

The Australian Securities and Investments Commission is separately investigating share trades worth more than $200 million that White made during a company blackout period. The company has previously said White obtained independent legal advice before undertaking the trades.

World.title: Prepared to ‘torpedo’ the season: Swans bosses apologise as five players banned
World.content:
Sydney chairman Andrew Pridham has apologised for the behaviour of the five players – Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, Riley Bice and James Jordon – who have been suspended for the rest of the season for breaching club behavioural standards. Pridham, whose board met on Tuesday night to decide on the sanctions, said the Swans’ preparedness to “torpedo” their premiership bid reflected how serious they were viewing the matter. Loading The penalties were reached independently of the Victoria Police investigation into an alleged sexual assault of a woman at the Pullman East Melbourne hotel on Monday morning. Appearing alongside club chief Matthew Pavlich at a 19-minute press conference on Wednesday, Pridham could not guarantee the quintet would play again for the Swans and defended coach Dean Cox, saying he had not done anything wrong heading out late with club staff on Sunday night.



Speaking publicly for the first time since the scandal engulfed the Swans, Pridham said the club was “deeply ashamed” by the actions of the five players. “At the outset, I want to offer an apology, sincere apology, to the community, to our many, many fans, to our corporate partners who’ve been amazingly supportive of us, understanding that we are attempting to deal with this matter as quickly as we can, as honestly as we can, given the constraints of the police inquiry, and to very much be transparent in our dealings with the media,” Pridham said. Swans CEO Matthew Pavlich and chairman Andrew Pridham front the media on Wednesday. George Chan “Our thoughts go out to everybody who’s been impacted by these events, and we know it’s impacted many, many people, ranging from the partners of our staff, our players, our women’s program, our men’s program. “There’s deep disappointment within the club at what has occurred, and we know that many people are hurting, and we are providing support to our players, to their partners, to as many people we can, to our fans and members.”



The Swans were in ongoing negotiations with the AFL over the penalties, according to a source with knowledge of the situation who was not authorised to speak publicly. They were aligned that the matter was serious. The AFL Players Association has been kept informed. The Swans said in a statement on Wednesday that the AFL was supportive of the club’s sanctions. Sydney Swans players Chad Warner, James Jordon, Isaac Heeney, Riley Bice and Nick Blakey. Marija Ercegovac By banning three of their best players for the rest of the season, the Swans have significantly dented their chances of winning their first flag in 14 years, but Pridham said the on-field implications were not a consideration for the board. Pavlich, Cox and football boss Leon Cameron also had input into the ban. “I think the fact that we’ve got to the place where we are today, and we’ve effectively suspended the players for the balance of season when we’re heading into a final series just tells you how seriously we’ve taken it.



“Clearly, something has gone wrong,” Pridham said. “They shouldn’t have been in that situation of being out that late. And the only way we can deal with it is to put our foot down incredibly hard, which we’ve done. “I think a very important point to make is that we, as a football club, that is our business, and to effectively torpedo our season by making a decision such as this just tells you how seriously we are taking it.” Asked if the five would play again for the club, Pridham said: “We just have to wait and see what happens going forward”. This masthead has contacted the representatives of Heeney, Bice, Jordon and Warner. This masthead also contacted a representative of Blakey, who stated Blakey was not involved in any incident. They confirmed Blakey had remained in Melbourne on Monday to travel back to Sydney by car later with his four teammates.



Related Article Investigation

AFL off-field behaviour A handful of Swans players wanted to keep partying. The fallout has rocked the AFL The players learnt of their penalties from Pavlich on Wednesday morning. “They’re incredibly disappointed in their actions,” Pavlich said. “They know they’ve let a lot of people down. They know they’ve impacted the women involved. They are remorseful about the hours of Monday morning, and we’ll get them back to the club and around their teammates and the staff at the right time.” Pavlich said the Swans had offered their support to the women but would not reach out to them out of respect for the police investigation. “We’re deeply concerned about their welfare and the wellbeing of those women,” Pavlich said.

World.title: Police allege homeowner was murdered after house guests locked him out
World.content:
A man and woman have been charged with murder after the 66-year-old owner of a house where the accused had been staying died of stab wounds. Emergency services rushed to the home on Lubach Street in Beenleigh about 4.45pm on Tuesday, following reports a man, later identified as Andrew Duncan Murray, had been assaulted and stabbed. Loading Neighbours and witnesses told reporters they heard screams and plates smashing. Police charged a 47-year-old Karalee builder, Lindsay James Kohn, with murder. His matter was briefly heard on Wednesday in the Brisbane Magistrates Court, where he did not appear.



His case was adjourned to September 23 in Beenleigh Magistrates Court, and he was remanded in custody. A 43-year-old Beenleigh woman, Jillian Greer Francis, was also charged with offences including murder and acts intended to maim or disfigure, after spending the night at hospital under police guard. Court documents list Francis’ occupation as a truck driver. Police at the scene of an alleged stabbing in Lubach Street in Beenleigh, where a 66-year-old man died of his injuries. Nine News Her case was heard in the Brisbane Magistrates Court, where she was remanded in custody. Magistrate Aaron Simpson also adjourned her case to September 23. Detective Inspector Ian Galpin said police would allege Murray had offered for Francis to stay in the home on a temporary basis about four months ago, with Kohn also living at the house on a part-time basis.



“Recently, the 66-year-old had asked these people to vacate his premises, and they had refused,” he said. “Things escalated [Tuesday] afternoon, when the 66-year-old found himself to be locked out of his home. Neighbours and witnesses told Nine News they heard screams and plates smashing. Nine News Police alleged Murray was stabbed after forcing his way into the house. Galpin said the older man was assaulted by both Francis and Kohn, and had been allegedly stabbed multiple times.



Local man Riley Sellars told Nine News he ran to the property after hearing commotion, and saw the man lying in a pool of blood. Police said Francis called Triple Zero, and officers and paramedics delivered first aid to the man, but he couldn’t be saved. When officers arrived they found a neighbour had entered the house and allegedly disarmed Francis and began giving the 66-year-old first aid. Galpin said the charge of acts intended to maim or disfigure related to an alleged attack by Francis on the neighbour. World.title: Viking lights up visual tungsten in drilling at historic Nevada mine
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Viking lights up visual tungsten in drilling at historic Nevada mine Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Andrew Todd August 19, 2026 — 1:23pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Viking Mines has hit the ground running at its Linka tungsten project in Nevada, USA, with maiden drilling intersecting multiple, wide zones of visual tungsten mineralisation in the first holes at the project in 40 years. The program marks the company’s first tilt at the target and early signs appear encouraging, with geologists spotting scheelite — the key tungsten-bearing mineral — lighting up under ultraviolet light in rock chips from the reverse circulation (RC) drilling. Strong visual scheelite mineralisation under UV light from drilling at Viking Mine’s Linka tungsten project in Nevada, USA. Viking says its strong hits feature disseminated, coarse-grained scheelite hosted in skarn rock over significant widths of up to 12m. Scheelite is the most important natural tungsten mineral for downstream production and is made up of about 80.5 per cent tungsten trioxide. Geologists on site are using its distinctive fluorescence under shortwave UV light to get an early read on the mineralisation ahead of laboratory assays. Key visual intercepts include a 12-metre continuous interval of visible scheelite from just 40m downhole in one hole, featuring estimated content of up to three per cent visual scheelite.



‘Initial visual mineralisation intercepts are highly encouraging and show multiple zones of strong disseminated scheelite.’ Viking Mines managing director and chief executive officer Julian Woodcock Another hole delivered a combined total of 13m of visible scheelite over a 19m-wide horizon from a shallow 9m depth. A third hole returned a combined 11m of visible scheelite from a 21m horizon starting at a mere 3m below surface. While management has rightly cautioned that visual estimates are no substitute for laboratory analysis, the initial results have provided plenty for the early imagination. The company says initial samples from the mineralised intercepts are being readied for dispatch to the lab, with the rig still churning away to deliver plenty more hits from the program. Viking Mines managing director and chief executive officer Julian Woodcock said: “Being on the ground at Linka observing our maiden RC drilling programme with the chip trays lighting up under the UV lamp hole after hole, as predicted by our 3D geological model, is as good as it gets prior to assays. These initial visual mineralisation intercepts are highly encouraging and show multiple zones of strong disseminated scheelite (CaWO4) mineralisation hosted in tactite over significant widths.” Viking’s Linka project comprises three historically producing tungsten mines that ceased operations in 1956, not for geological reasons, but due to a slump in the tungsten price. With the global tungsten market continuing to grapple with a severe supply squeeze, the rapid run-up in prices has thrust the company’s Nevada assets into sharper focus as Western supply chains hunt for secure, reliable tungsten sources.



European benchmark prices for ammonium paratungstate, a key intermediate tungsten product, averaged an eye-watering $US3075 (A$4400) per metric ton unit in the second quarter of 2026 - a more than sixfold jump from just twelve months earlier. The historic mill grade of approximately 0.5 per cent tungsten trioxide ranks Linka amongst the higher of comparable global tungsten projects, as the brownfields project continues to show its restart opportunity chops. Historic infrastructure, including a 46m shaft, historic pits and underground workings across a tungsten trend of up to 1.6km, has the company focused on near term production at today’s record high prices. Management has already proposed an early-stage plant design with flexibility at its core. The modular processing flowsheet could allow for future additions, suggesting a capital-light, disciplined and staged development plan for early production. With the rods still turning on site and the first batch of samples now being prepared for dispatch to the lab in Reno, assays are expected in four to six weeks. For Viking and the punters alike, the wait for that maiden set of numbers will likely be keenly anticipated. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting?
